# HANDBOOK
## OF ETHICS,
### Containing the Principal
## Rudiments of MORAL PHILOSOPHY,

->Illustrated for the most part by the records of the Ancients, and perpetually adapted to the integrity of life.<- <note>The "monuments of the Ancients" refers to the surviving writings and philosophical traditions of Greek and Roman thinkers.</note>

->By<-

## **HENRY MORE**
### of Cambridge.

->To which is added the Author’s Letter to a Most Illustrious Man.<- <note>original: "Epistola ad V. C." — V. C. stands for Vir Clarissimus, a formal Latin honorific used for distinguished scholars or gentlemen.</note>

# TO THE READER.

<image-desc>Ornate woodcut decorative initial 'N' featuring the letter intertwined with thick foliage and vine patterns within a square border.</image-desc>

There is no reason why I should delay you long, friend Reader, for the sake of a preface; although I ought not to pass you by again entirely ungreeted, unless even then, when I am writing about **Morals**, I myself should wish to appear ill-mannered. <note>The author is making a play on words in Latin between *Moribus* (Ethics or Morals) and *male moratus* (badly mannered or immoral).</note> Therefore, just as I have done in most of my writings—so that the Reader may understand what the **Occasion**, what the **Goal**, and finally what the **Reason** for writing each of them was—I thought the same should be done briefly in this present little work.

With how unwilling and reluctant a mind I approached whatever this work is, those very people know who urged me with such great effort to undertake it. For many things stood in the way, preventing me from allowing myself to be overcome even by their most vehement and frequently repeated demands. One reason was that I am the sort of person who was not accustomed to grant much value to dry and meager systems of **Moral Philosophy** <note>In this period, "Moral Philosophy" was the standard term for what we now call Ethics.</note> of this kind, which strive to battle against solid **Vice** and **Baseness** with the mere "shadow-boxings" <note>original Greek: <term>σκιομαχίαις</term> (*skiomachiais*), referring to fighting an imaginary enemy or hitting the air.</note> of **Definitions** and **Divisions**. For Vice...

## To the Reader.

...for I thought that **Vice** must be conquered by **Virtue** alone; however, I believed that true and living **Virtue** cannot be taught, but must be drawn through **Faith** in God, from the living God and His living **Oracles** <note>In a 17th-century theological context, "Oracles" refers to the Holy Scriptures.</note>. For there must be a certain divine sense <note>The author refers to a spiritual intuition or "moral sense," a concept central to the Cambridge Platonists.</note> underlying it; he who possesses and nurtures this, and does not knowingly and willingly violate or wound it, will at last easily judge, as if of his own accord, what is honorable or shameful in every matter. 

But he who is deprived of this sense, however well-instructed he may be in all manner of **Distributions** and **Definitions** of the **Virtues**, will nevertheless never arrive at true **Virtue**; nor, since he has not yet stripped off his [old] self, will he recognize what true **Virtue** is, nor perhaps even believe it to be anything more than an empty name. With which kind of monsters (alas!) almost all places are filled in this age.

The second reason was that I had recently devoted my time and mind to certain most pleasant studies, from which I was very reluctant to be so suddenly torn away; especially since, after my strength had been undermined and dried up by certain recent labors—and those a bit more intense than usual—[I was enjoying] the gentle and dewy breeze of these new speculations...

## To the Reader.

...reflecting upon this very thing, I—the same man who yesterday so bravely repelled those external darts—immediately succumb, pierced by the internal stings of **conscience** <note>Latin: *conscientiae*</note>. # *To the Reader.*

...extraordinary, for I thought that [evil] must be defeated by **Virtue** <note>original: *Virtute*</note> alone; but that true and living Virtue cannot be taught, but must be drawn through **Faith** <note>original: *Fidem*</note> in God from the living God and His living **Oracles** <note>original: *Oraculis*; here referring to the Holy Scriptures or divine revelations.</note>. For there must be an underlying **Divine sense** <note>original: *Divinum sensum*</note>; he who possesses and nurtures this, and does not knowingly and willingly violate or wound it, will at last easily judge for himself what is **honorable** <note>original: *honestum*</note> or **shameful** <note>original: *turpe*</note> in any matter, as if by his own accord. But he who is destitute of this sense, however well-instructed he may be in all kinds of **Distributions and Definitions of Virtues** <note>original: *Virtutum Distributionibus & Definitionibus*; likely referring to the scholastic or academic categorizations of ethics used in universities at the time.</note>, will never arrive at true Virtue, nor—as he has not yet stripped off his [selfish] self—will he know what true Virtue is; perhaps he will not even believe that it is anything more than an empty name. With this kind of monster—alas!—nearly every place is filled in this age.

The second reason [for my hesitation] was that I had recently devoted my time and mind to certain most pleasant studies, from which I was very reluctant to be torn away so suddenly; especially since, after my strength had been shaken and dried up by certain recent labors—labors a little more intense than usual—I was being refreshed by the gentle and dewy breeze of these new **speculations** <note>original: *speculationum*; in this context, theoretical or philosophical contemplations that the author found more enjoyable than the hard work of moral philosophy.</note>...

### To the Reader.

Reflecting on this very thing, I—the same man who just yesterday so bravely repelled those external darts—now immediately succumb, pierced by the internal stings of conscience. For among other things, this bit and burned my mind sharply: that unless I now—while I am being swept away in another direction by such a great rush of pleasure—immediately set myself to this work (in which at least some hope of public benefit shines forth), I could not be certain whether, in all those labors I have exhausted so far in writing, the consideration of the **Pleasant** <note>original: *Jucundi*; referring to the aesthetic or personal satisfaction of writing.</note> rather than the **Honorable** <note>original: *Honesti*; referring to moral duty and the public good.</note> had perpetually driven me. Nor could I be sure that my works were the fruits of true Virtue, rather than the effects of a certain <term>Cacoëthes</term> <note>From the Greek *kakoēthes*, a medical term used by classical authors like Juvenal to describe an "itch" or "malignant habit"—here, an uncontrollable urge to keep writing.</note> for scribbling. To such an extent that the very thing which previously held me back most strongly now most violently of all impelled me to undertake this present work. And the more unpleasant the task seemed, the more obstinately I attacked it, so that it might be more clearly established to my own satisfaction that my sincerity was genuine.

But in truth, to confess frankly how things stand: once I had outlined the scope of the whole work in my mind (which I did in a very short space of time) and had finished a part of it, the undertaking began to please and flatter me so much that, although certain things happened in the middle of my progress

->### To the Reader.<-

...things which at other times might have forcibly held me back, I nonetheless could not then abandon my undertaking, nor set down my pen, until I had completed the work I had begun. To be perfectly frank, this also added a "spur to the running horse" <note>original: *currenti calcar addidit*; a classical idiom for urging on someone who is already moving at full speed.</note>. I believed it was entirely fitting for a man who had worked so diligently to lay the primary and most vital foundations of <term>Natural Theology</term> <note>The study of God based on reason and the observation of nature, rather than on divine revelation.</note>—specifically by demonstrating that ***God exists*** and the ***human soul is immortal***—to now build this third part concerning ***Life*** and ***Morals*** upon those very foundations. Such was the occasion for this work.

The goal, however—not of the writer (for mine, as I have said, is simply to fulfill the duty of my own conscience), but of the writing itself—is the same goal that all works on **Ethics** should share: namely, the improvement of human life. For many people seem to fall into the error of thinking that ethical systems are created only to air useless trivialities. They treat ***moral discipline***—as **Cicero** <note>Marcus Tullius Cicero (106–43 BCE), the Roman statesman and philosopher whose works on duty were foundational to Western ethics.</note> puts it—as a "display of knowledge, rather than a law for living." Yet the true and genuine purpose of **Moral Philosophy** is that, by reading its precepts...

->### To the Reader.<-

...I felt myself to be wonderfully refreshed and soothed.

Finally, I argued that this effort would be unnecessary, since a certain man—most excellent and learned, as they themselves know—was already planning a most perfect *Ethical Work on that primary Question concerning the immutable principles of Good and Evil* <note>original: *Opus Ethicum de primaria illa Quæſtione circa immutabiles Boni Malique rationes*. This likely refers to Ralph Cudworth, a fellow Cambridge Platonist, though his work on the subject was not published until much later.</note>; a work which, I said, I hoped would soon be published. I strongly pressed these arguments against them.

They, however, replied that it would be of the greatest importance in these times if someone were to arrange such *Ethical Elements* <note>original: *Rudimenta Ethica*; basic principles or foundational teachings of morality.</note> in so clear an order and derivation that the reasoning behind all the Precepts <note>original: *Præceptorum ratio*; the logic or "the why" behind moral rules.</note> would be easily plain to anyone. For such is the spirit of the present age: people demand the Causes of all things, and they argue that the human Mind is bound by nothing except <term>Right Reason</term> <note>original: *Recta Ratio*; a central concept in this era's philosophy, referring to the innate human capacity to perceive universal moral truths through logic and divine light.</note>. A work of this kind, so skillfully crafted, would greatly delight the virtuous, and would successfully instill those divine feelings of the soul in those who perhaps lack them.

Furthermore, as far as those more "pleasant" studies are concerned <note>The author likely refers to his more abstract metaphysical or poetic interests.</note>, they can be set aside for a time and resumed later: nor should private...

Finally, as for the scholarly labors <note>original: *Lucubrationes*; literally 'work done by lamplight,' implying intense, late-night study and intellectual effort.</note> of that most excellent Man; although they knew well enough that they would be most accurate and extensive, it was nevertheless uncertain—given his many varied affairs—when they would be finished or sent to the press. They said they truly desired a *System of Ethics*; yet not a full-sized Volume, but rather a <term>Handbook</term> <note>original: *Enchiridion*; a Greek-derived term for a small, portable manual intended to be 'at hand' at all times for ready reference.</note>, a small book, easily carried, and well-suited for instructing <term>Beginners</term> <note>original: *Tyronibus*; novices or students who are just beginning their education in a specific subject.</note>.

We debated back and forth on these points at great length. Yet at that time, I felt myself by no means defeated or moved by their arguments. I believed it would be perfectly justified if I allowed no excuse to call me away from those studies in which I found such delight, and through which I felt the strength of my mind and body so wonderfully restored and refreshed. Indeed, I did not think it possible that I could be shifted from this position by any "engine" <note>original: *machinis*; here used metaphorically to mean powerful arguments or persuasive devices.</note> of persuasion.

And yet, on the following day—see the uncertainty of human plans!—while lying in bed early in the morning after waking, and turning the memory of these matters over in my mind...

From this source, then—the point just mentioned—the entire rationale for this writing must be derived. By "rationale," I do not mean a specific <term>Method</term> <note>The author is distinguishing between the formal structure of the argument and the underlying spirit or "genius" of the book.</note>, whether **Synthetic** <note>original: *Syntheticam*; a method of reasoning that builds from simple parts to a complex whole.</note> or **Analytic** <note>original: *Analythicam*; a method that breaks down a complex subject into its component parts.</note>, but rather the very form and character of the entire work. Nevertheless, as far as that "Method" properly so-called is concerned, I have by no means neglected it, even if I did not think I should bind myself too severely or restrictively in that matter. Always, however, as far as I recall, that which is clearer precedes, and that which is more obscure follows. This single principle encompasses the essence of nearly every pedagogical method.

As for why I have not scraped together and piled up every detail that might seem necessary for a complete **System of Ethics**, I have deferred to <term>Prudence</term> <note>original: *Prudentiæ*; practical wisdom or the ability to judge the best course of action.</note>. For I confess that I have seized every opportunity to display before the eyes of the **Christian World** that holy sense of **Virtue**, which was so deeply seated even in the minds of the <term>Pagans</term> <note>original: *Ethnicorum*; referring to the non-Christian classical philosophers of Greece and Rome.</note>, and which they testified to so clearly through those divine sayings and opinions they committed to writing. It is right that we Christians should be ashamed that there are so few among us who are found to live as justly or to speak as wisely; indeed, we have been so blinded that we trample upon and despise both the reality and the name of **Virtue**—as if by deliberate effort—as if it were something vile and profane, to be left to the **Barbarian Nations**. In doing this, however, we do not insult foreign nations so much as we display our own gross ignorance.

--- Page 18 ---
<meta>This page continues from the previous page's discussion of virtue as a participation in the Divine Nature. It completes the sentence "For although [various names] occur..." and concludes the author's preface.</meta>

[...various names] occur, such as ***Virtue***, ***Grace***, and the (so-called) ***Divine Life***; yet if anyone looks more deeply into these things, they will find them to be exactly the same. Indeed, this **perfection of the Mind** is called the ***Life of God*** insofar as it is a *living* image of Him within us—not a light and superficial notion or imagination of **Virtue**, but rather a solid and persistent sense and embrace of the most beautiful things. It is called ***Grace***, however, insofar as it is a free gift of God. Finally, it is called ***Virtue***, as it is a certain power of the **Mind** by which we so master the bodily **Passions** that in every matter we constantly pursue what is absolutely best, just as we have defined it in the following **Treatise**. I certainly thought it worthwhile to give this warning, so that I might here confront the foul and ruinous error of certain people who, while ***Uprightness*** is exiled <note>original: *exsulante Probitate*. The author is criticizing those who claim to be "spiritual" or "saved" while behaving immorally.</note>, nevertheless think they can keep the ***Divine Life*** at home with them, and who, under the pretext of ***Grace***, cast ***Virtue*** out of doors.

## Preface to the Reader Concerning this Second Edition.

<margin>1.</margin> Lest you should perhaps think, dear Reader, that I have accomplished more in this Second Edition than I actually have, I decided I should briefly explain to you what I have done in it.

<margin>2.</margin> First, then, I have not decorated or enriched this new Edition of our <term>Enchiridion</term> <note>From the Greek word for a "handbook" or manual; in this context, it refers to More's *Enchiridion Ethicum* (Manual of Ethics).</note> with any new opinions or information, although it presents you with more Chapters in the first Book than that previous Edition. For I have divided the fourth Chapter into two, and the seventh into five; this was done so that readers might have more frequent opportunities to pause and reflect; and so that from the distinct Titles or Summaries that I have placed before each Chapter, a somewhat easier and clearer understanding of the matters taught might arise.

<margin>3.</margin> Second, I have rendered into English <note>original: *Latine* (Latin). In this Latin text, More explains he has translated Greek quotes into Latin for the reader's convenience. *Extension—which we can in no way erase from our minds without it existing—must necessarily, according to the mind of <term>Descartes</term> <note>original: *Cartesius*; referring to René Descartes, whose mechanical philosophy Henry More initially admired but later critiqued.</note>, be corporeal. And certainly, even from this one argument that now occurs to me, taken from the motion of the **Earth**, it will be clear to anyone whose intellect is neither slow nor occupied by great prejudices, that this necessity of existing belongs not indeed to the extended matter of the **World**, but to some other immaterial **Extension**. For there are no **Speculations** in the whole of **Philosophy** (not even **Mathematics** itself excepted) of which I am more certain in mind and knowledge than this one which I now propose. *Indeed, we have touched upon this same opinion in many places throughout this very Letter. ### Preface to the Reader.

*Since this much-vaunted **Mechanical Philosophy** <note>The 17th-century view that all physical phenomena can be explained by matter in motion and mechanical laws, like a clock.</note>, which is now so widely celebrated, so miserably hallucinates regarding simple things—things so bare on all sides, so easily understood by our minds, and perfectly transparent—how mad, I ask, is the hope, and how insane the promise, that anyone could devise purely mechanical causes for all things that appear in the **World** <note>original: *Mundo*</note>, even those that consist of the greatest and most intricate craftsmanship? This seems to me not unlike the impudence and recklessness of one who, having capsized a small two-bench boat in the harbor, nevertheless boasted that he could pilot the ship of the **Argonauts** <note>In Greek mythology, the Argo was the large, complex ship used by Jason to find the Golden Fleece.</note> across the **Black Sea** <note>original: *Euxino Ponto*</note>. Just as **Lucius Crassus** <note>A famous Roman orator and statesman (140–91 BCE).</note> reasons both skillfully and soundly in his own case within the works of **Cicero** <note>The Roman statesman and philosopher Marcus Tullius Cicero.</note>.*

16. *As for what concerns me, I am of the opinion that not only can those most intricate **Phenomena** <note>Observable events or facts.</note> not be explained by purely mechanical principles, but that **nothing** can. But now (which I have done not out of any levity or inconstancy of mind, but overwhelmed by the weight of reasons), I have changed my opinion and called it home <note>i.e., retracted his previous stance.</note>. ### Concerning this Second Edition

*There is, I think, no one who has a mind preoccupied by no prejudice, who would not prefer to **acknowledge one and the same homogeneous Principle everywhere**, rather than one that is different in various places and discordant in its entire nature. # HANDBOOK
## OF ETHICS.

### CHAPTER I.
#### *What Ethics is.*

Ethics is the <term>Art of living well and happily</term> <note>original: "Ars bene beateque vivendi." In this period, an "art" referred to a systematic body of knowledge or a practical skill guided by rules.</note>.

1. By <term>Art</term>, I mean a methodical grasp of <term>homogeneous precepts</term> <note>original: "Præceptorum homogeneorum"; rules or principles that are all of the same kind or nature, specifically pertaining to the same subject matter.</note>: and therefore, since the *Art* we are treating here is *Ethics*, it is necessary that all its Precepts be truly Ethical, and rightly lead toward the attainment of its goal; otherwise, they would not be *homogeneous*. For this reason, one should not expect to find any precepts here that serve useless disputation, but only those which serve the proper ordering of life.

I say, *of living well and happily*; because a person can live *well*, even if they do not live quite so *happily*. The <term>Pythagoreans</term> <note>Followers of the ancient Greek philosopher Pythagoras; the author likely refers to Neopythagorean texts that distinguished between internal virtue and the outward fulfillment of life.</note> also rightly distinguished between these states of human life. For, according to their doctrine, it is one thing to be *perfect according to nature*, and another to be *perfect according to life*.

<note>The distinction between "living well" (acting virtuously) and "living happily" (achieving a state of blessedness or fulfillment) is a central theme in classical moral philosophy.</note>

2. Those who are *perfect by nature* are those who are endowed with <term>Virtue</term> <note>original: "Virtus." In this context, virtue refers to moral excellence and the functional perfection of the human soul.</note>. For Virtue is, as they define it, *the summit and perfection of each thing's nature*. However, these people they call <term>merely good</term> <note>original: μόνους ἀγαθούς (monous agathous), meaning "only good" or "good alone."</note>, but not yet <term>blessed</term> <note>original: "beatos." For they define <term>Happiness</term> <note>original: "Beatitudinem."</note> as the Perfection of human life; and human life they define as a <term>collection of human actions</term> <note>original: σύστημα τῶν πράξεων (systēma tōn praxeōn), literally a "system of actions."</note>. For <term>Virtue and Fortune together</term> bring actions to perfection: Virtue indeed as far as their *practice* is concerned, but the goods of Fortune as far as their *success* is concerned, as **Hippodamus the Thurian** <note>A 5th-century BCE Greek philosopher and architect associated with the Pythagorean school.</note> rightly and soundly concludes.

3. With this also agrees the opinion of **Archytas** <note>A Greek philosopher, mathematician, and statesman of the Pythagorean school.</note>, who defines <term>Happiness</term> as *the use of virtue amidst prosperous Fortune* <note>original: "Χρῆσιν ἀρετᾶς ἐν εὐτυχίᾳ" (Chrēsin aretas en eutychia).</note>. ## CHAPTER II.
### *On the Parts of Ethics, and on Happiness.*

1. **T**here are two parts of Ethics: the *Knowledge of Happiness* and its *Acquisition*. *Knowledge* contains the teaching on the nature of Happiness, and of those things which its nature touches upon or embraces in at least some way. But in truth, as *Aristotle* has confessed very often, although it is easy to establish in this manner that "that which is in harmony with Right Reason is best," nevertheless, defining exactly what this Right Reason is, or what its measure might be, seems the most difficult task of all. For in the *Great Ethics* <margin>Book 2, chapter 10.</margin> <note>Aristotle's *Magna Moralia*</note>, when asking what and where this Right Reason is, the matter finally comes to this: *Unless you have a sense for such things within yourself, nothing is achieved.* This is the answer of a physician when asked in what way the paleness of a feverish patient is detected. But the Philosopher immediately adds: *The situation is similar in judging the Passions: for one must grasp a conjecture, as it were, from a sense.* Ultimately, then, judgment is resolved into *a certain internal Sense*; which I would certainly call the <term>Boniform faculty of the soul <note>From the Latin "boniformis," meaning "good-shaped." This is Henry More’s term for a specific power of the soul that senses and delights in moral goodness directly, much like the eye senses light.</note></term>. However, it must be admitted that anyone who is moved in this way seems <term>to experience something similar to those who are divinely inspired <note>original Greek: ὁμοιόν τι πάσχειν τοῖς ἐνθυσιάζουσι (homoion ti paschein tois enthousiazousi)</note></term> (as *Aristotle* notes elsewhere <margin>Ethics, Book 2, chapter 8.</margin> regarding those who are carried toward the Good by a certain natural impulse and without reason), being affected in the same way as those who are breathed upon by the divine Power. And certainly this principle, which I call <term>Boniform <note>original Greek: ἀγαθοειδές (agathoeides), meaning "God-like" or "having the form of the Good"</note></term>, is the most divine thing in us of all, yet the least "fanatical" or irrational of all.

In the first place, God, the supreme Commander, issues decrees. But that [Contemplation] is that for the sake of which Prudence itself exists, which He thus engenders in the minds of men. This Prudence itself also determines what is best in human affairs.*

### Certain Noemata <term>Noemata <note>From the Greek word for "thoughts" or "conceptions." ### Noema III.

*Among the species or degrees of perceptive lives found throughout the universe, some are more superior and excellent than others.*

### Noema IV.

*One **Good** <note>original: Bonum</note> can be superior to another by nature, by duration, or by both.*

This is clear in itself. It can, however, be illustrated by the absurdity that would follow otherwise: one life would not be more excellent than another, nor one happiness greater than another. Thus, God, an angel, a human, a horse, and the lowliest little worm <note>original: vermiculus</note> would be equally happy. No one, unless they are completely insane, can admit this in any way. Regarding **Duration**, not even the slightest doubt or difficulty can arise.

### Noema V.

*That which is **Good** is to be chosen; but **Evil** <note>original: malum</note> is to be avoided. Furthermore, a superior good is to be chosen over that which is less superior; and a lesser evil is to be endured so that we do not undergo a greater one.*

### Noema VI.

*In that which we ourselves have not yet experienced*

### Noema XIII.

> *We ought to pursue the highest and most absolute Good with the highest affection, moderate things with moderate affection, and the least things with the least; nor should we subordinate the highest Good (or those Goods related to it) to moderate or least things, but rather we must subordinate the moderate and least to the highest.*

### Noema XVII.
*It is good for a person to have the means by which they may live well and happily.* <note>original: "Bonum est homini ut habeat unde bene beateque vivat." This axiom establishes that basic well-being and the resources for happiness are inherently good things for an individual to possess.</note>

### Noema XVIII.
*If it is good that one person should have the means to live well and happily, it follows from a certain and clearly Mathematical Analogy that it is twice as good for two people to have such means, three times as good for three, a thousand times for a thousand, and so on.* <note>Here, More uses "Mathematical Analogy" to argue for what we might now call the "greatest good for the greatest number." He treats morality like geometry—if a unit of happiness is good, then more units are objectively better.</note>

### Noema XIX.
*It is better for one person to live without luxury than for another to live in calamity and misery.* <note>original: "Melius est unum hominem non voluptuoſe vivere, quam alterum calamitoſe ac miſere." This is a foundational principle of social justice: preventing suffering takes ethical priority over providing extra pleasure or "voluptuous" living for others.</note>

### Noema XX.
*It is good to obey the <term>Magistrate</term> in <term>indifferent matters</term>, even without any fear of punishment.* <note>The "Magistrate" refers to the civil government or legal authority. "Indifferent matters" (original: <term>adiaphora</term>) are actions that are not inherently right or wrong by divine law—such as which side of the road to drive on or specific tax rates. More argues we should obey these laws out of a sense of moral duty, not just because we are afraid of getting caught.</note>

### Noema XXI.
*It is better to obey God than to obey men or our own personal desires.*

### Noema XXII.
*It is good and just that what belongs to each person should be given to them, and that they should be permitted to use and possess it without harassment.* <note>original: "suum cuique tribuatur"—to each his own. This is the classical definition of distributive justice: respecting private property and the rights of the individual.</note>

### Noema XXIII.

> *It is clear, however, that a person may behave in such a way that what belongs to them by acquisition or gift ceases to be theirs by right.* <note>original: "Manifestum tamen est, quod ita quis se gerere possit, ut quod acquisitione vel donatione suum est, de jure desinat esse suum." 4. You might rightly call these and similar **Sayings** by the name **Moral Truths** <note>original: <term>Noemata Moralia</term>. More uses "Noemata" to describe self-evident moral axioms that the mind perceives as immediately true, much like the axioms of geometry.</note>, as they are so clear and manifest in themselves—provided one is willing to consider them without prejudice—that they require no circuitous reasoning or long chains of arguments, but are recognized as true at first glance. We now have a ready answer for anyone asking what **Right Reason** <note>original: <term>Recta Ratio</term></note> is: for it is that which, through certain and necessary consequences, is finally resolved into some **Intellectual Principle** <note>original: <term>Intellectuale Principium</term></note> that is immediately true. If anyone should further ask for an example of such principles in the field of Morals, those we have just listed are ready at hand.

### Noema XVII.
*It is good for a human being to have the means by which they may live well and happily.* <note>original: "Bonum est homini ut habeat unde bene beateque vivat." This axiom asserts that having the basic resources for a flourishing life is an inherent good.</note>

### Noema XVIII.
*If it is good for one person to be supplied with the means to live well and happily, it follows from a certain and clearly **Mathematical Analogy** <note>original: <term>Analogia Mathematica</term></note> that it is twice as good for two people to be so supplied, three times for three, a thousand times for a thousand, and so on.* <note>More applies quantitative logic to morality here, suggesting that the "Good" increases proportionally with the number of people who enjoy it—a precursor to later utilitarian thought.</note>

### Noema XIX.
*It is better for one person to live without luxury than for another to live in calamity and misery.* <note>original: "Melius est unum hominem non voluptuose vivere, quam alterum calamitose ac misere." This principle establishes a moral hierarchy: preventing suffering is a higher priority than providing pleasure.</note>

### Noema XX.
*It is good to obey the **Magistrate** <note>original: <term>Magistratui</term></note> in **indifferent matters**, even without any fear of punishment.* <note>The term "indifferent matters" (<term>adiaphora</term>) refers to actions that are not inherently right or wrong by divine law (such as which side of the road to drive on). More argues that social order justifies obedience even when the law isn't backed by an immediate threat.</note>

### Noema XXI.

### Noema XXIII.

> *It is nevertheless manifest that a person can so conduct themselves that what belongs to them through acquisition or gift may, by right, cease to be theirs.* <note>original: "Manifeftum tamen eft, quod ita quis fe gerere poffit, ut quod acquifitione vel donatione fuum eft, de jure definat effe fuum." 4. These and similar sayings you might rightly call <term>Moral Axioms</term> <note>original: <term>Noemata Moralia</term>. If one further seeks an example of such principles in the field of Morals, those we have just now reviewed are close at hand.

Furthermore, simple self-preservation <term>conservatio</term> <note>original: *conservatio suiipsius*. More is likely responding to thinkers like Thomas Hobbes, who argued that self-preservation is the primary driver of human action.</note> is not desirable in itself, since it can be weighed down by such great misery or foulness that it would cause anyone—except the most foolish—to become utterly weary of life.

And if this kind of preservation for one man is good, then for two it is twice as good, for three it is three times as good, and so on; so that, according to the light of Nature <term>lumen Naturæ</term> <note>The "Light of Nature" refers to innate human reason, which More believes is a God-given tool for discovering moral truths.</note>, it follows that every Intellectual Creature <term>Creatura Intellectualis</term> <note>A being capable of rational thought, encompassing humans and higher spiritual beings.</note> is bound to care for and promote the preservation of both themselves and their neighbor, both now and in the future, as much as they are able, and as far as it can be done without injury to a third party. This indeed fulfills no small part of *Justice* <term>Justitia</term>, as well as of *Temperance* <term>Temperantia</term> and every Virtue <term>Virtus</term> whatsoever.

### CHAPTER VII.
### *Concerning the Passions, specifically so-called.*

1. Since no one, as far as I know, has enumerated the types of passions more accurately than that distinguished philosopher ***Descartes*** <note>original: *Cartesius*—René Descartes (1596–1650), the French philosopher whose 1649 work "The Passions of the Soul" revolutionized the psychological and physiological study of emotions.</note>, nor defined them more clearly, I will almost always follow in his footsteps in this matter, unless some significant reason prevents me. Otherwise, it will not be out of place first to offer a fuller definition of ***Passion*** <note>original: *Passio*—in this context, an emotion or internal movement of the soul.</note>, and to place it before the specific types that follow.

2. A ***Passion*** is therefore a vehement ***Sensation*** of the soul which is specifically referred to the soul itself, and is joined with an extraordinary motion of the ***spirits*** <note>original: *spirituum motu*—referring to "animal spirits," which early modern thinkers believed were extremely fine fluids or vapors that traveled through the nerves to allow the soul and body to communicate.</note>. ***Sensation*** is rightly called ***Passion***, because in a passion the soul feels that it is being acted upon <note>original: *pati*—the Latin root of "passion" literally means "to suffer" or "to be a passive recipient" of an action.</note>; and it is called ***vehement***, because it acts with great force. Furthermore, this sensation is said to be ***referred specifically to the soul itself*** so that it may be distinguished from other sensations; some of these are referred to external objects, such as smells, sounds, and colors; others to our own body, such as hunger, thirst, and pain. Finally, I say this sensation is ***joined*** with the motion of the spirits, rather than produced by it; for the former always happens, while the latter does not always occur—indeed, perhaps it is rarer, if you exclude that motion which arises from food and drink, or a change in the air. For in the case of external objects by which the senses or the imagination are struck, the soul moves the spirits, not the spirits the soul.

<summary>In this chapter, Henry More adopts René Descartes' framework for defining the passions, characterizing them as intense sensations where the soul perceives itself as being acted upon. He distinguishes these emotional "passions" from external sensory perceptions (like color) and internal bodily sensations (like hunger) based on their relation to the soul's own movement.</summary>

# Chapter 7. Manual of Ethics.

<margin>On the Passions of the Soul, Part 2, Article 69.</margin>

3. ***Descartes*** <note>original: *Cartesius*</note> reduces all the Passions of the Soul to six principal and primary types: ***Wonder*** <note>original: *Admirationem*—In 17th-century philosophy, this refers to the initial surprise or "wonder" at something new, rather than just high regard.</note>, ***Love***, ***Hatred***, ***Desire***, ***Joy***, and ***Sadness***. Their order and distinction are understood by this logic: For as soon as any new object, or an object modified by some new circumstance, meets us, it halts and detains the soul's power of observation and carries it away into an extraordinary state of attention; this is ***Wonder*** itself. Since this can happen before we know whether the object will be pleasing or unpleasing, this passion must rightly be considered the first of all.

4. Afterward, however, if the soul considers the object under the aspect of the pleasing or the unpleasing—which signifies almost the same thing as good or evil—it excites either ***Love*** or ***Hatred***. Moreover, if this good and evil are considered as future things, they kindle ***Desire*** within us; the former is a desire for uniting with it or possessing it, the latter a desire for avoiding it or removing it from ourselves. The Scholastics <note>The "Schools" or Scholastic philosophers, medieval academics whose terminology More often critiques or refines.</note> call the first ***Longing*** <note>original: *Desiderium*</note> and the second ***Aversion*** <note>original: *Fuga*—literally "flight" or "escape."</note>; and certainly not without reason. Finally, if they are considered as present, Good produces ***Joy***, and Evil produces ***Sadness***.

5. But, although ***Descartes*** seems to me to have calculated quite correctly in this list of Passions, I do not see why they could not with equal right be reduced to a shorter number—namely, to those first three,

13. **Hope** is a *Passion of the soul by which it is disposed to believe that what it desires will happen*: **Fear**, however, *is that by which it is disposed to believe that what it desires will not happen*. **Hope** that excludes all fear is called **Security**, or **Confidence**; whereas **Fear** that excludes all hope is called **Despair**. **Jealousy** <note>original: *Zelotypia*</note> is the **Fear** of losing a good we value highly, arising from even the slightest causes of suspicion.

14. **Fluctuation of the soul** is the **Fear** of erring in the choice of means toward some intended goal. **High-spiritedness** <note>original: *Animositas*—in this context, it refers to a vigorous, courageous drive to act, rather than the modern sense of "hostility"</note> is the **Passion** which disposes the soul to act manfully in the execution of things it is preparing for. If this is seen in matters accompanied by some great danger, it is called **Boldness** <note>original: *Audacia*</note>; but if it is excited by considering the success of others, it is called **Emulation** <note>original: *Aemulatio*—a healthy desire to match the excellence of another</note>.

Opposed to **High-spiritedness** is **Faint-heartedness** <note>original: *Pusillanimitas*—literally "smallness of soul"</note>, just as **Dismay** <note>original: *Consternatio*</note> is opposed to **Boldness**. Indeed, **Faint-heartedness** is a certain weak and cold Passion of the Soul, which hinders it from being carried toward accomplishing those things it could otherwise do. **Dismay**, however, is **Faint-heartedness** joined with disturbance and stupor, which takes away from the soul the power of resisting an imminent evil.

<margin>The Fourth Class of Passions.</margin>
15. The fourth class consists of **Joy** and **Sadness**, which regard a present good or evil. The passions which are reduced to this class—

### Chapter 7. Manual of Ethics.
-> Page 47 <-
<meta>catchword: of good</meta>

...[they are] distinguished by these principal circumstances. First, in simple respect to ourselves or to others. For a present Good, as it regards ourselves, produces **Joy** <note>original: *Gaudium*</note>, and an Evil produces **Sadness** <note>original: *Tristitiam*</note>. If an evil happens to another who is worthy of it, it produces **Derision** <note>original: *Irrisionem*—pleasure taken in the deserved misfortune of another</note>; if to one who is unworthy, **Pity** <note>original: *Commiserationem*</note>. If, however, a good comes to one who is unworthy, it produces **Envy** <note>original: *Invidiam*</note>; but a good happening to another which also redounds in some way to our own benefit produces **Congratulation** <note>original: *Congratulationem*—a sense of shared joy</note>.

16. Furthermore, Good and Evil are considered—whether they regard us or others—first, by reason of their cause. For a Good performed by ourselves produces **Satisfaction** <note>original: *Satisfactio*</note> or **Peace of Mind** <note>original: *Animi Acquiescentiam*—literally the soul's resting in itself</note>, while an Evil produces **Repentance** <note>original: *Poenitentiam*</note> and the **Sting of a Doubting Conscience**. But a Good performed by others produces **Favor**, even if it was not done for us; if, however, it was done for us, it produces **Gratitude**. Likewise, an Evil committed by others, if it is not committed against ourselves, produces only **Indignation**; but if it touches ourselves, it produces **Anger** <note>original: *Iram*</note>.

Again, they are considered in respect to the opinion of others. A Good which we possess excites in us **Glory** <note>original: *Gloriam*—here meaning a sense of honor or justified pride</note>, while an Evil excites **Shame** <note>original: *Pudorem*</note>.

Finally, they are considered in respect to time. A long-lasting Good produces **Satiety** <note>original: *Satietatem*</note> or **Weariness** <note>original: *Fastidium*—a sense of loathing born from excess</note>, just as the long duration of an Evil diminishes **Sadness**. From a past good is born **Longing** <note>original: *Desiderium*</note> properly so-called, and from a past evil, **Cheerfulness** <note>original: *Hilaritas*</note>.

17. **Joy** is a pleasant commotion of the soul, or a **Passion**, in which consists the **Enjoyment** <note>original: *Fruitio*—the act of possessing and taking pleasure in the fruit of one's efforts</note> of a good...

### Manual of Ethics. Book I.
<meta>catchword: themselves</meta>

...of a good which the soul conceives as its own. **Sadness** <note>original: *Tristitia*</note> is an unpleasant passion of the soul, which consists of the discomfort of an evil or a defect which the soul conceives as its own. **Derision** <note>original: *Irrisio*</note> is a Joy arising from the perception of some slight evil in a person who is thought to deserve it. If it arises from greater causes and is joined with a more open desire to inflict insult, it is more correctly called **Insulting** <note>original: *Insultatio*—a form of mocking triumph over another's misfortune</note>. **Envy** <note>original: *Invidia*</note> is a Sadness arising from the consideration of a good happening to someone who is unworthy of it. **Compassion** <note>original: *Commiseratio*—also translated as Pity</note> is a Sadness arising from the consideration of some evil that happens to one who is unworthy. **Congratulation** <note>original: *Congratulatio*</note> is a Joy arising from a good coming to someone else, which we nevertheless consider to be in some way in our own interest. **Satisfaction** or **Self-Contentment** <note>original: *Satisfactio* or *Acquiescentia in seipso*—literally "the soul's resting in itself"</note> is the most pleasant Joy of all, proceeding from the opinion of some deed that one has recently performed. **Repentance** <note>original: *Pœnitentia*</note> is the most bitter Sadness of all, arising from the consciousness of some evil committed. **The sting of conscience** <note>original: *Morsus conscientiæ*</note> is a Sadness arising from a doubt whether what we have done be good or not. Moreover, it is the effect of rashness, when we undertake some work before all hesitation or wavering of the mind has been set aside.

18. **Favor** is a certain joyful benevolence toward those in whose right actions we take delight. **Gratitude** <note>original: *Gratitudo*</note> is a certain joyful desire to do good to those who have done good to us. **Indignation** <note>original: *Indignatio*</note> is a Sadness kindled against those who have done something evil. **Anger** <note>original: *Ira*</note> is indignation against those who [have done] some evil to our very selves...

### CHAPTER VIII.
### *The Use and Interpretation of the Passions; and first of Wonder with its Class, and of the remaining five primitive Passions.*

1. As for what concerns the **Ends and Uses of the Passions** <note>original: *Fines Ususque Passionum*</note>, it will not be out of place to pursue them somewhat more at length, and to interpret the voice of Nature in all of them as faithfully as I can. For it will be of no small importance for the right moderation and use of the **Passions** <note>In the 17th century, "Passions" referred to what we now call emotions or affects—internal movements of the soul triggered by external stimuli</note> (which is certainly the greatest part of **Virtue** <note>original: *Virtutis*</note>), if we understand to what end Nature, or the **Parent of Nature, God**, has destined each one, and how highly he esteems his own works, or wishes them to be esteemed by others. But these things are said in passing regarding the Affections that relate to the body. Let us return to the **Passions** properly so called, and weigh their Ends and Uses in roughly the order we previously proposed.

3. First, therefore, concerning **Wonder** <note>original: *Admiratione*. In 17th-century philosophy, "Wonder" was considered the first of the passions, triggered by the sudden surprise of the soul when faced with something new or unexpected</note>, it is clear that it serves to more strongly impress the observations of new things upon the memory, so that the soul, being sufficiently equipped with this storehouse of information, may arrive at the knowledge of the most useful truths. Hence, if anyone is gripped by the desire of contemplating new things for the sole purpose of wondering at them, he clearly loses the purpose of this Passion, and turns into a mere **Gawker** <note>original: *Mirionem*. A Latin term for someone who is perpetually amazed by trifles but lacks the intellectual depth to understand them</note>.

# Manual of Ethics. Book I.
<meta>catchword: spur</meta>

Because Nature has instilled in us the passions of *Esteem* and *Contempt* <note>original Latin: *Existimatio* and *Despectus*</note>, she suggests that not all things are to be held by us at the same value. But if there is a "worse" and a "better," surely that which is best is the goal to which we ought, with Nature as our guide, to aspire.

4. *Self-Esteem* is a Passion mixed from *Wonder*, *Joy*, and *Love* of one's own condition. *Self-Contempt*, however, is mixed from *Wonder*, *Sadness*, and *Self-Love* combined with *Hatred of one's own defects*. Both Passions suggest that every human being either is, or ought to be, something of value, and should be held in such a regard as to be above all injury and contempt. For since we are so easily led to believe ourselves to be "something," even though we do not differ so much from others; surely it is fair that we also consider other people to be "something" and treat them humanely and dutifully. Therefore, humanity and civility of manners—as well as diligence and industry in attaining the best things—are pointed out to us by Nature through these Passions.

5. Regarding that specific kind of *Self-Esteem* which **Descartes** <note>René Descartes (1596–1650), a French philosopher whose work on the "Passions of the Soul" deeply influenced More's ethical system</note> calls *Generosity* <note>original: *Generositas*. In this context, it refers to "nobility of spirit" or "magnanimity" rather than just being charitable with money</note>, by which a person values themselves based on the sincere use of their free will, and believes they ought not to be despised so long as they follow **Virtue** as perfectly as they can, and do not lack the will to undertake and carry out whatever right **Reason** prescribes; surely the use of this Passion, which Nature has instilled in us, is the most remarkable of all, since so great a [spur]...

# Manual of Ethics. Book I.

...be directed toward objects which are not in our power; nor should it be carried with a more violent impulse toward those things which are, than this frail and mortal body can endure.

For to desire those things which are in our power to be completed more hastily than our strength allows would be just as if we were once again entangled in those things which are simply not in our power. Hence, this unhealthy **Desire** <note>original: *Cupiditas*</note> would produce not so much alacrity as anxiety and torment.

Finally, since it is so clearly evident what the purpose <note>The "end" or final cause in Aristotelian terms.</note> of **Desire** is—namely, to kindle our strength for the execution of a Purpose—this **Passion** must be set aside entirely, except when we are "in the trenches" <note>original: *in procinctu*; a military idiom for being ready for immediate action.</note> to carry out what we have decided to do. Otherwise, this useless ardor (especially in those with a more delicate physical constitution), by over-inflaming the spirits <note>The author refers to "animal spirits," thought to be the fluid messengers of the nervous system.</note>, will exhaust one's strength, dry out the body, and greatly harm its health.

### CHAPTER X.
### *The Use and Interpretation of the Third Class of Passions, which Desire leads.*

1. The primary types of **Desire** <note>original: *Cupiditas*; a broad term for longing or the drive toward an object.</note> are *Hope*, *Fear*, *Jealousy*, *Security*, and *Despair*; the others are *Fluctuation of Mind*, *Spirit* <note>original: *Animositas*; here meaning a vigorous or courageous spirit rather than modern "animosity."</note>, *Boldness*, *Emulation*, *Faint-heartedness*, and *Consternation*.

2. *Hope* is composed of **Joy** and **Desire**, while *Fear* is composed of **Desire** and a certain **Sadness**. For Imagination is a kind of weak sensation, as *Aristotle* says; yet Sensation is concerned with things present, as are Sadness and Joy. Future events, however, are present to the mind even though they are not present in reality; and therefore they are both present and absent, and can be the objects of *Joy* or *Sadness* just as much as they are objects of *Desire*. The use of *Hope* is that we may be enticed to act; the use of *Fear* is that we may act cautiously and diligently.

3. There is, however, a certain special and primary use of this Passion which relates to political matters. Since the greatest part of men... <note>The text cuts off here, leading into a discussion on how fear and hope govern social and political behavior.</note>

4. **Jealousy** <note>original: *Zelotypia*; in this context, it refers to a protective zeal or intense concern for something one values, rather than just romantic envy.</note> is composed of **Desire**, **Sadness**, and **Esteem**. Its proper use is seen in the caring for and guarding of matters of the greatest importance. Hence, to apply it to things of little value would be both dishonorable and ridiculous.

5. From which Passions **Security** and **Despair** are composed is quite clear from the preceding remarks: since **Security** is nothing other than **Hope** free from all fear; and **Despair** is nothing but **Fear** stripped of all hope. The use of the former is as a remedy against excessive or unnecessary worry and diligence. The latter serves to pull the mind away from a project that will not succeed, so that it may be turned toward things that have a better chance of success.

6. **Fluctuation of Mind** <note>original: *Fluctuatio animi*; the psychological state of wavering or hesitation between two choices.</note> is composed of **Desire** and **Sadness**. Its purpose is to ensure we do not make mistakes when choosing between options. The distress that accompanies this state is a sign from Nature that one thing is far superior to another, and that we must promptly apply all our effort to perceive what is truly best, and what means are most suited to achieving or keeping it. In this way, we may build our lives upon deliberate and fixed Principles and Judgments, from which we have resolved within ourselves—with a steady and certain mind—never to depart.

7. **Spiritedness** and **Boldness** <note>original: *Animositas* & *Audacia*</note> are both composed of **Desire**, **Joy**, and **Sadness**; however, they are combined in such a way that **Joy** greatly outweighs **Sadness**. While **Sadness** arises from the danger being faced, that danger is almost entirely disregarded because of the excellence of the goal being pursued; **Joy**, meanwhile, arises from the certainty of attaining that goal. The primary use of this passion is in liberating one's Homeland or Sovereign from enemies, and in bearing witness to the Truth—even at the extreme risk of our lives—so that we may achieve either immortal glory or eternal life.

8. **Emulation** is composed of **Desire**, **Joy**, and **Esteem**. Its use is seen in the noble examples of the Virtues, which Nature stimulates us to imitate through this passion. **Faint-heartedness** <note>original: *Pusillanimitas*; literally "small-souledness," referring to a lack of spirit or resolve.</note> seems to be composed of all these elements: **Desire**, **Hope**, **Fear**, and **Esteem**, but at a very low intensity. Its chief use concerns objects of surely little value, even if they are perhaps held in no small regard by some. **Consternation** <note>original: *Consternatio*; a state of paralyzing shock or panic.</note> is composed of immense **Wonder** <note>original: *Admiratione*; in early modern philosophy, this refers to a profound surprise or shock at the unexpected.</note>, **Desire**, and **Sadness**. It appears to be a kind of reproach and warning from Nature of how shamefully we lack that presence of mind with which we ought always to be girded and armed against all the unexpected incursions of **Fortune**. Its use and significance are almost the same as those of **Fluctuation of Mind**: to ensure that, with our reasons well-calculated, we have ready at hand what must be done in each and every case.

#### *The Interpretation and Use of the Passions of the Fourth Class, which consist of Joy and Sadness.*

Moreover, the **Object of Laughter** is, as **Aristotle** (if I recall correctly) notes somewhere, "a non-destructive evil" <note>original: κακὸν μὴ φθαρτικὸν (*kakon mē phthartikon*); see Aristotle's *Poetics* 1449a.</note>, or a misfortune that is by no means fatal. 3. Therefore, in these instances, its object is good. And it is so even in a sense where the evil is not overcome—that is, where the situation is not set right—provided the loss is of no great consequence. For *a small evil bears the character of a good*. <note>This is a common philosophical maxim: compared to a greater catastrophe, a minor mishap is a relative "good" or a relief.</note> Thus **Laughter** appears as the voice of Nature applauding herself: though there is an unbridled and slippery tendency of Matter toward great and manifold misfortunes, **Divine Providence** <note>original: *Consilio Divino*</note> has so provided that they result only in very light and tolerable mishaps. This certainly, and with good reason, stirs up Joy.

4. **Compassion** <note>original: *Commiseratio*</note> is a mixture of Love and Sadness. Its use is clearly directed toward helping the miserable and upholding **Justice**, so that no innocent person is subjected to extreme punishment; for such a monstrous deed would tear at the very vitals of Nature herself and draw groans and sighs from the hearts of all mortals. **Indignation** <note>original: *Invidia*—while often translated as "envy," the author here uses it in the Aristotelian sense of righteous indignation at the unmerited success of others.</note> is composed of Sadness and Hatred. Its usefulness is primarily related to the correct distribution of rewards and honors. For this Passion is not that vice which everyone rightly condemns, but a most excellent emotion given by God. **Aristotle** himself noted more than once that this is called **Nemesis**, <term>derived from the distribution to each according to their due</term> <note>original: ἀπὸ τοῦ ἑκάστῳ διανεμήσεως (*apo tou hekastō dianemēseōs*)</note>. He contends in his *Rhetoric* that it is the duty of a good man to feel pain for those who are undeservedly unfortunate and to pity them; but to feel indignation—or "envy"—toward those who are undeservedly fortunate. <margin>Book 2, chapter 9.</margin> "For that which happens contrary to merit is unjust," he says; "hence we attribute this indignation even to the gods themselves." Yet this is the very same Passion as the **Indignation** we defined above.

From these Passions, therefore—**Compassion** and **Indignation**—we are warned, as if by the voice of Nature herself, that there is something just and unjust, or fair and unfair; and that the latter must be avoided, while the former must be embraced.

5. **Congratulation** <note>original: *Congratulatio*; here meaning the act of rejoicing in another's good fortune</note> is composed of Love and Joy, and it can serve as a stimulus for common **Beneficence**. For to the person who excels in this virtue, the shared **Congratulation** of all people is owed as a reward for their prosperity.

**Satisfaction**, or **Self-Contentment** <note>original: *Acquiescentia in seipso*</note>, as well as **Repentance** and **Remorse of Conscience**, all clearly work toward the preservation of a good Conscience. Furthermore, they point most clearly to the distinction between Good Deeds and Bad Deeds, and prove that we are endowed with **Free Will**. For this **Contentment** or **Satisfaction** is nothing other than a certain applause and exultation of the soul arising from the consciousness of a right action. This emotion would certainly be quite senseless if there were no such things as actions done rightly and actions done otherwise. However, it must be admitted that most men at times hallucinate most foully regarding the object of this Passion, applauding themselves most highly for a "deed well done" even when they have committed the most atrocious crimes.

Regarding **Repentance** <note>original: *Pœnitentia*</note>, if all things happened by **necessity** <note>original: *necessario*; the philosophical concept of determinism, where humans have no choice in their actions</note>, every sorrow arising from the consciousness of a bad deed would be just as ridiculous as if a Peasant repented for not being born a Nobleman, or a woman for not being born a man. For these Passions arise from the fact that we judge that some things are done rightly by men, and others wrongly.

8. **Gratitude** indeed seems to be a certain natural part of **commutative justice** <note>original: *Justitia commutativa*; the fairness required in private dealings and exchange of goods</note>; just as **Compassion**, **Envy**, **Favor**, and **Indignation** can be seen as natural parts, so to speak, of **distributive justice** <note>original: *Justitia distributiva*; the fair allocation of rewards and punishments within a society</note>. **Anger** itself stands out beyond the others. For **Vengeance** is a conspicuous part of punitive justice, which the **Pythagoreans** <note>followers of the philosopher Pythagoras, known for their focus on mathematics and harmony</note> placed primarily in **retaliation** <note>original Greek: <term>ἐν τῷ ἀντιπεπονθόti</term> (en tō antipeponthoti); the principle of "suffering the same in return" or reciprocity</note>, as **Aristotle** testifies.

**Anger** also contributes to **Fortitude** <note>courage or moral strength</note>, just as **Boldness** and **Spiritedness** do; as that quite elegant sentiment of **Theages** <note>a Pythagorean philosopher</note> suggests: *For **Anger** and **Desire** are so ordered toward the ruling part of the Soul, that the one acts as its bodyguard and guardian of the body, while the other is the steward and caretaker of necessities.* He compares Desire to a Provisioner <note>original: *opsonatori*; a caterer or buyer of food</note>, and Anger to a Soldier.

Therefore, whoever devotes himself entirely to the motions of the **Concupiscible** <note>the faculty of the soul dealing with simple desires, pleasures, and the avoidance of pain</note> faculty, under the pretext of some sort of peace and sweetness, should beware lest he turn out to be a traitor to Piety and the public good. For if someone completely discards the **Irascible** faculty, he is either crafty, or soft, or both, and he will never be able to be **an adequate spearman and faithful bodyguard of virtue** <note>original Greek: *doryphoros hikanos kai pistos somatophylax tes aretes*</note>, (as **Theages** <note>a Pythagorean philosopher to whom several ethical treatises were attributed</note> puts it), that is:

> *A true guardian and rigid attendant of Virtue.*

10. There is also a most excellent use for **Glory** <note>original: *Gloria*</note> and **Shame** <note>original: *Pudor*; often translated as a sense of modesty or the fear of disgrace</note>. For the former stimulates us to accomplish all things noble; the latter calls us away and deters us from disgraceful things, so much so that it is like a certain Citadel and Rampart of Virtue. **Glory** is composed of Joy, Self-Love, and Esteem; **Shame** is composed of Sadness, Self-Love, and a certain measure of Contempt. Hence, **Shame** is found neither in the worst of men nor in the best <note>More implies that the "worst" are beyond shame, while the "best" (the perfectly virtuous) have no cause for it</note>.

For he who is conscious within himself that he constantly employs his free will toward those things which are best, knows that he ought not to be despised; and thus, rising above all contempt, he himself despises the very act of being despised. This constitutes a great part of **Generosity** <note>original: *Generositas*; in this philosophical context, it refers to "nobility of spirit" or the Cartesian idea of high-mindedness based on the correct use of free will</note>. In the wicked, however, we see the very summit of **Baseness** <note>original: *Improbitas*; a lack of moral integrity or a state of being "un-approved"</note>; for a kind of impunity for sins seems granted to those who can endure both disgrace and infamy without feeling any pain.

<margin>Cicero, *Tusculan Disputations*, Book 4.</margin>

11. There is, therefore, a fairly straightforward interpretation of these Passions—namely, **Shame** <note>original: *Pudor*</note> and **Glory** <note>original: *Gloria*</note>. Both indicate that we should abide by the common judgment of mankind rather than merely our own private opinion. This contributes greatly not only to the grace of our manners but also to **Political Obedience** <note>original: *Obedientia Politica*; the willingness of a citizen to follow the laws of the state</note>. For by this natural instinct, we are taught that no private individual should commit any act against the **Laws** <note>original: *Leges*</note>, since, as **Aristotle** <note>384–322 BCE; the Greek philosopher’s definition of law here emphasizes its role as a collective moral testimony</note> defines it, “The law is the testimony of the sentiment or opinion of the whole people regarding matters, indicating how each thing ought to be done.” Furthermore, that natural shame or **Modesty** <note>original: *Verecundia*</note> concerning bodily pleasures warns us that such pleasures are not truly worthy of human excellence, and thus ought to be disdained and rejected—a point which **Cicero** <note>106–43 BCE; the Roman statesman and philosopher often discussed the tension between virtue and sensory pleasure</note> skillfully suggests in his writings.

<margin>Aristotle, *Rhetoric*, Book 1, Chapter 1.</margin>

<margin>2.</margin> For this Law of Nature <note>original: *lex Naturæ*</note> ruling in the Animal Region <term>Animalis Regio: in More’s philosophy, this refers to the lower part of the human soul governed by instincts and sensations shared with the animal kingdom</term> is like a certain confused murmur and whisper of a certain more divine law, whose voice is much more articulate in the Intellectual Region <note>original: *Regio Intellectualis*</note>. In this lower Region, however, that state of the case frequently occurs which is called by Legal Experts a *missing case* <note>original: *Casus omissus*; a legal term for a situation or set of facts not covered by existing statutes, requiring the judge to apply broader principles of equity</note>. Whence frequent Appeals must be made to the Tribunal of Reason <note>original: *Rationis Tribunal*</note> concerning the time, the measure, and the other circumstances of Actions. For such is the nature of Reason, that it judges both more *distinctly* and more *separately* than the Animal Light <term>Lumen Animale: the natural, unthinking instinct or "inner light" that guides biological life</term> or the Law of Passions <note>original: *Lex Passionum*</note>. It judges *more distinctly*, as it is the faculty that can examine the natures of things and their circumstances, whereas Passion is only a blind and indefinite Impulse toward a thing without any knowledge of the thing's nature. It judges *more separately* and abstractly, as it is the faculty which does not seek what is good or pleasing to this or that person, but what is simply good or better, and what ought to be pleasing or more pleasing in given circumstances.

<margin>3.</margin> For this is the character of every Intellectual faculty, as I advised above: to perceive and define not what is true or good to this or that person, but what is simply true or good. From this it is manifest, that whatever is Intellectual and truly Moral <note>original: *Morale*</note>, is something divine...

5. For from this Principle it would immediately follow that one could rightly and lawfully devastate with fire not only his own house, but the entire city where he lives, by secretly setting torches to the buildings at night, poison public wells, slaughter his wife and children, or gouge out their eyes and cut off their hands and noses, for no reason other than that it is pleasing to him, and he is thus sacrificing to a present Passion. Since this Foundation is the falsest of all and most foreign to human nature, it follows immediately that an individual’s own Emotion is not the measure of good or evil, but that the Emotions themselves must be limited by some other Principle.

# Ethical Handbook. Book I.

6. Now, the next Principle by which the Passions are limited, and which knows how to define what is good or evil in specific circumstances, is *Reason*. Truly, whatever appears good or evil to right Reason is, in reality and by its very nature, good or evil. For this Reason, when correctly conceived by our mind, is the "formal reason" <note>original: *formalis ratio*; in scholastic philosophy, this refers to the defining essence or the objective logic of what a thing is</note> of the thing itself, or its nature or essence represented to the mind; just as the nature or essence of a Triangle is that which right Reason represents to itself.

7. From this it is clearly evident that there are certain fixed Notions or Ideas of Good and Evil, just as there are of Figures in Mathematics. The Emotion <term>Affectus: often translated as "affections" or "emotions," these are the movements of the soul's desires</term> does not define these any more than the Senses define geometric figures; rather, Reason and the Intellect circumscribe both. They define the latter [mathematical figures] from a specific drawing and arrangement of lines, and the former [moral ideas] from the proper or improper meeting of circumstances, from which various types and names of good and evil arise. From this it is finally clear, as I have said, that the Principle by which Moral good and evil is judged is Intellectual, and in a certain way, Divine.

8. Since this is the case, one cannot help but perceive that something Divine is hidden even in the Animal Law <term>Lex Animalis: the basic biological instincts or "animal" nature of humans, which remains a part of God's creation</term> (which proceeds from Nature and from God, the Parent of Nature), and that we ought always to follow its indications, unless something better is judged to be so, once all emotion and prejudice have been set aside. Once this single point is granted (which no one but a madman could deny), an infinite harvest of examples will grow from it.

# Chapter 13. Ethical Handbook.

...[tempe]rament and *Habit*; or to *Education*, <term>personal disposition <note>original Greek: ἰδιοπάθειαν (*idiopatheian*); refers to an individual's unique physical or emotional constitution that colors their perception</note></term>, or *Self-centered Feeling*, and <term>partiality <note>original Greek: *Prosopolepsiam*; literally "respect of persons," meaning a bias or prejudice based on external appearances</note></term>. Impressions of the first class agree in this: that they are considered apart from any passion properly so-called. Those of the second class are accompanied by some passion properly so-called. By *Sensation* I mean here not the act of sensing itself (which is the proper meaning of the word), but that defect and crooked inclination toward error which it impresses upon the soul. And the same applies generally to the others.

2. Therefore, ***Sensation is a bodily Impression by which the Soul is inclined to think that things are, in their own nature, exactly as they appear to the external sense.*** As if someone, because they noticed something pleasing to their *Taste*, should immediately conclude that that sweetness or deliciousness exists in the very thing they are tasting, and consequently that it would be equally pleasing to the tastes of all, both beasts and men.

The same fallacy seems to be forced upon the soul in *Sight*, when it thinks that the light or colors it perceives are truly in the objects themselves which it sees; whereas it is just as false as if one thought that the pain felt in the feet while walking over rough ground was in the stones themselves, or that the heat felt from touching a warm object was in that warm object being touched. For Heat is no more in the object than Pain is, since both are created by the agitation of particles. <note>The author is following the "New Philosophy" of the 17th century (like that of Descartes or Boyle), which argued that "secondary qualities" like color, heat, and taste are not in the objects themselves, but are sensations produced in us by the motion of matter.</note>

<summary>This page defines Sensation not as a neutral act of perceiving, but as a bodily impression that often misleads the soul into attributing subjective qualities (like taste or color) to external objects. It argues that heat and color are as subjective as pain, being products of the "agitation of particles."</summary>

# Ethical Handbook. Book I.

Therefore, heat and pain differ only in degree, and consequently, they exist in the same subject—that is, within ourselves. And so it is with the rest of the objects of the external senses.

3. ***Imagination is a bodily Impression by which the Soul is inclined to believe those things either exist or will be, which nevertheless neither exist nor ever will.*** Just as *Sensation*, unless the soul is on its guard, easily leads it into error regarding the natures of things, so *Imagination* leads it into error regarding their existence, whether present or future. For just as the vigor of *Sense* makes us certain of the real presence and existence of some thing, so the intensity of Imagination—which can in a way equal or at least imitate Sensation itself—easily forces upon the soul a false certainty that a thing is true or will be so, for no other reason than that it is so vividly imagined. 6. *Custom is a bodily Impression, by which the soul is strongly inclined to judge things to be true, or good and becoming, solely because it has become accustomed to thinking so, and to acting according to this opinion, when otherwise no reason for so thinking or acting would exist.* A most illustrious instance of this depravity is found in the <term>Anthropophagi</term> <note>original: *Anthropophagis*; literally "human-eaters" or cannibals</note>, who feed on human flesh without any horror. Therefore, care must be taken early on that we do not accustom ourselves to evil or false things, nor mingle in the society of those who are imbued with bad habits or perverse opinions. *For the sense of good things is gradually worn away and washed out by conversation and familiarity with wicked men.*

# BOOK TWO.

### CHAPTER I.

#### *On the Number of Primitive Virtues.*

1. Thus far we have treated *Virtue in general*, and the *Passions*, along with other *bodily impressions*. Now follow the *Virtues in specific*. Some of these, just like the *Passions* themselves, are <term>Primitive<note>In this context, "primitive" means primary or foundational—the root virtues from which others grow.</note></term>, and others are *Derivative*. The *Primitive Virtues* are three: *Prudence*, *Sincerity*, and *Patience*. These in some way correspond to and follow the three *Primitive Passions*, serving as either their perfections or their corrections: *Prudence* corresponds to *Admiration* <note>original Latin: *Admirationi*; here meaning a state of wonder or being struck by the novelty of a thing.</note>, *Sincerity* to *Desire* <note>original: *Concupiscentiæ*; an intense longing or appetite for something.</note>, and finally *Patience* to *Irascibility* <note>original: *Excandescentiæ*; literally "a glowing heat," referring to a sudden flare-up of anger or passion.</note>.

<note>The author classifies these three virtues as "primitive" because they directly regulate the three basic emotional responses of the human mind: our wonder, our wants, and our anger.</note>

To show that we have not stumbled upon this triad of Virtues by chance, but rather that Nature and right Reason have pointed them out to us, I thought it would not be out of place to bring to light what is found on this subject among the ancient writers. For they quite often seem to indicate this summary number of either Virtues or Duties, even if they do not distinguish them by the exact same names. But as they agree in substance, they sufficiently indicate that this first three-part division of Virtues is very natural.

2. *Metopus the Pythagorean* <note>Metopus was a philosopher of the Pythagorean school, likely from the late Hellenistic period, known for his work on virtue.</note> suggests that there are three Virtues based on the three parts of the Soul. He calls the first the <term>Rational<note>original Greek: τὸ λογιστικὸν (*to logistikon*); the part of the soul responsible for logic and reasoning.</note></term>, the second the <term>Irascible<note>original Greek: τὸ θυμοειδὲς (*to thymoeides*); the "spirited" part of the soul, which handles emotions like anger, courage, and the drive to overcome obstacles.</note></term> (*which he describes as a kind of defensive and protective faculty against things that are close at hand*), and the third the <term>Appetitive and Concupiscible<note>original Greek: τὸ ὀρεκτικὸν καὶ ἐπιθυμητικὸν (*to orektikon kai epithymētikon*); the parts of the soul related to basic desires, needs, and physical cravings.</note></term>. In the beginning of that Fragment, he says: *It is necessary for every Virtue to possess these three: Reason, Power or Strength, and Appetite or Choice. Reason, indeed, by which it judges and contemplates; Power, by which it resists and conquers; and finally Appetite, by which it loves and embraces something.* Our three primitive Virtues correspond most clearly to these.

3. *Theages* <note>Another Pythagorean writer, often associated with the work "On the Virtues."</note> also enumerates these same parts, adding furthermore: *The virtue of the Rational part of the soul is Prudence, while that of the Irascible part is Fortitude. For it is the habit of resisting and enduring heavy burdens.* And

# Ethical Handbook. Book II.

### CHAPTER II.
### On the first Primitive Virtue: Prudence.

1. *Prudence*, therefore, is a **Virtue** of the soul by which it so rules over the **Passions** (properly so-called) and over all bodily **Impressions** that they do not prevent the **Mind** from discerning clearly in every deliberation, and successfully discovering what is absolutely and simply the best. From this it appears there is a certain versatility of intellect in *Shrewdness* which cannot be lacking in a prudent man; this is due to the refinement of the spirits <note>More refers to the "animal spirits," which in 17th-century thought were subtle fluids that served as the medium between the soul and the physical body.
