Moreover, since this *Shrewdness* is present, <term>Good Counsel<note>original Greek: εὐβουλία (euboulia); Latin: *felix Consilium*</note></term> cannot be absent either; as the Philosopher <note>That is, Aristotle.</note> defines it, this is *Rightness of counsel that prescribes that which is good*.

<margin>Eudemian Ethics, Book 5, Chapter 9, and Nicomachean Ethics, Book 6, Chapter 10.</margin>
In *Good Counsel*, it is generally required that the end be honorable, the means be lawful, and the deliberation be neither headlong nor too slow. By the definition of *Prudence*, these qualities will easily be understood to reside in a prudent man. For a prudent man, being the master of his emotions, will always observe that precept of *Antoninus* <note>The Roman Emperor Marcus Aurelius, whom More frequently cites as a moral authority.</note>, <term>Do not act at random<note>original Greek: Μὴ εἰκῇ ὁρμᾶσθαι (Mē eikē hormasthai)</note></term>; and through the purification of his spirits, he will be neither slow nor headlong (for their refinement and purity contribute to Gentleness and Patience). Much less will he attempt unjust things, or seek just things through unjust means, since these are usually done by those who indulge their passions and are led astray by them.

For if anyone does something right without it, that should surely be attributed not so much to Virtue as to Chance or Fortune.

11. Furthermore, **Sincerity** or **Simplicity** <note>original: *Sinceritas* or *Simplicitas*; meaning a singleness of heart and honesty of purpose.</note> cannot be missing from the Virtues, without which they should be considered not so much Virtues as certain shadows or lifeless images of Virtues. For if something is so mixed with honest deeds that without that extrinsic and accidental end it is uncertain whether they would have ever been started or completed, it is manifest that deeds of this kind have utterly lost both the name and nature of **Virtue**. For this would not be to pursue what is simply and absolutely best, but what is most useful to oneself and most pleasant to the animal life <note>The "animal life" or "animal nature" refers to the lower instincts, physical desires, and self-preservation, as opposed to the higher "divine" or rational life.</note>. Which is not the duty of Virtue, but the impulse and cunning of the animal nature. Since, on the contrary, what is true, simple, and sincere is most suited to the nature of man—that is, most in harmony with Reason—as **Marcus Cicero** <note>The Roman statesman and philosopher Cicero.</note> rightly advises us.

<margin>On Duties, book 1.</margin>
12. Finally, **Patience** <note>original: *Patientia*</note> least of all can be missing from a good man, since without it there is no security at all for the remaining Virtues. For he who is soft or ambitious, or the slave of any animal affection <note>original: *animalis affectus*; a passion or emotion rooted in the lower physical self.</note>, can be faithful to no one—not to his Prince, not to his Country, not to Religion, not to Friends, not [to himself]...

1. 4. *Cicero*, in the first book of *On the Laws*, delineated that Natural Law in words that are truly quite magnificent, yet true and apt: *In establishing Right, let us take our beginning from that supreme Law which was born in all ages before any written Law, or before any state was established at all. Because, moreover, the nature of the immortal God wishes all divine nature to be ruled by reason, power, mind, and divine will (as our own soul openly professes), in that he has opened to us the fountain of the best and most perfect Law.*

*For what is there*, he says, *I will not say in man, but in all heaven and earth, more divine than Reason? Which, when it has matured and been perfected, is named Wisdom. It is therefore...*

4. Finally, it is the duty of private individuals or equals—or rather of everyone—to help each other mutually when needed, to stand by agreements, and to act in good faith toward one another, never seeking one’s own advantage through the disadvantage of another.

## Ethical Handbook. Book II.

5. That famous *Division of Justice* into distributive and corrective <note>original: *διανεμητικὴν & διορθωτικὴν* (dianemētikēn & diorthōtikēn). Distributive justice concerns how goods are handed out, while corrective justice concerns how wrongs are righted.</note> belongs especially to Political science. In these divisions, we understand that Aristotelian concept of "equal justice" <note>original Greek: *τὸ ἴσον δίκαιον* (to ison dikaion)</note>, and that *Justice* is a kind of *equality*. However, the equality which Justice seeks is that seen in proportion. For proportion, or analogy <note>original: *ἀναλογία* (analogia)</note>, is the *equality of ratios* <note>original Greek: *ἰσότης τῶν λόγων* (isotēs tōn logōn)</note>.

6. Furthermore, Analogy or Proportion is either *Geometric* or *Arithmetic*. Geometric proportion occurs when four magnitudes or numbers are compared such that the third contains the fourth (or is contained by it) as many times as the first contains the second (or is contained by it). For example, in 2 to 6 and 4 to 12, or in 6 to 2 and 12 to 4 <note>In both cases, the ratio is 1:3 or 3:1.</note>. This proportion pertains to *Distributive Justice*. For as one person is to another person—say, *Ajax* to *Achilles* <note>Two Greek heroes from the Trojan War; because Achilles was the greater warrior, distributive justice suggests his rewards should be proportionally higher than those of Ajax.</note>—so should one honor relate to the other honor. This is the equality of proportion. If merits were equal, then rewards should be equal not only in ratio, but in magnitude.

7. *Arithmetic* proportion occurs when four numbers or magnitudes are compared such that the same excess or deficit exists between the first two as exists between the last two; that is, there is an equality of difference on both sides. For example, in 5, 7, 9, 11 <note>In this sequence, the difference between each number is exactly 2.</note>. This pertains to *Corrective Justice* <note>In corrective justice, the law seeks to restore the balance by removing the exact amount of "gain" from a wrongdoer and restoring the "loss" to the victim, regardless of their social status.</note>.

Though, to confess frankly how the matter stands,

### Chapter 6. Ethical Handbook.

[...Arithmetic proportion] is, an image of this *Arithmetic* proportion is not so easily detected in *Corrective Justice* <note>original: *Correctiva Justitia*; the branch of justice concerned with righting wrongs and compensating victims.</note> in a sufficiently expressed distinction of four terms of this kind. For the equal excesses or defects are not drawn from the number of terms themselves, which nonetheless *Andronicus of Rhodes* <note>original: *Andronicus Rhodius*; a 1st-century BCE philosopher who edited Aristotle's works and wrote on ethics.</note> seems to suggest. 

<margin>Book 5, chapter 5.</margin>
But if we wish to devise four terms, it seems necessary that we establish the first two as both the one to whom the injury was brought, and the one who brought the injury; but by this reasoning, so that it is understood that an appeal to the Judge has not yet been made, nor a sentence passed against the defendant. However, insofar as the injured party later becomes the Plaintiff <term>original: *Actor*; the party bringing the legal action</term>, and the one who caused the injury becomes the Defendant <term>original: *Reus*; the party being sued or accused</term>, two other terms emerge. After the sentence is passed by the Judge, that excess which exists between the injured party and the one who caused the injury is inverted; that is, that good which one unjustly took from the other is transferred to the other two in such a way that, just as the one who caused the injury surpassed the other in this good, so, after the sentence is passed, he is surpassed by that same good in the same way. That is, he is fined or diminished in good as much as he had despoiled the other. Hence it is necessary that the Plaintiff <note>the *Actor*</note> surpass the Defendant <note>the *Reus*</note> by as much as the one who committed the injury had surpassed the injured party, or at least that they are made equal: which is clearly an *Arithmetic* proportion.

<margin>Book 5, chapter 5.</margin>

### CHAPTER VII.
### *On the remaining two Principal Derivative Virtues, Fortitude and Temperance.*

1. Fortitude <note>or Courage</note> and Temperance <note>or Self-Control</note> agree in this: that they look more immediately to ourselves; although their utility, just as with all other Virtues, can also be applied to one's neighbor, and in some way overflow into that which they call *Universal Justice*. <margin>Book 5, chapter 1.</margin> For to use all Virtues for the benefit of one's neighbor—this is justice, says the *Rhodian Paraphrast* <note>original: *Paraphrastes Rhodius*; referring to Andronicus of Rhodes, a 1st-century BCE philosopher who created popular summaries of Aristotle's work</note>. 2. What *Fortitude* <note>or Courage</note> truly is will become easily clear from the description of a *Brave* man, found both in the works of *Cicero* and *Aristotle*.

#### *Concerning the Reductive Virtues.*

The nature of the three principal *Derivative Virtues* has been explained, and their justifications from the *Intellectual Principles* have been briefly indicated.

4. **Liberality** <term>Liberality: The virtue of being generous and sensible with one's money and possessions.</term> is concerned with the use of money. Indeed, the use of money is nothing other than the spending and giving of it.

<margin>Andronicus of Rhodes, Book 4, chapter 1.</margin>
If, therefore, someone spends gladly and cheerfully **in proportion to their wealth** <note>original Greek: *κατ’ ἀναλογίαν τῆς οὐσίας* (kat’ analogian tēs ousias)</note>—at the right time, on the right things, and for the right purpose—that person is **liberal**. One who gives without measure or discrimination is **prodigal**; one who gives below this law and measure is **illiberal** <note>meaning stingy or lacking the spirit of a free person</note>.

5. **Magnificence** <term>Magnificence: Distinct from simple generosity, this virtue involves large-scale spending for the public good or high honors.</term> is also concerned with spending, but only with large expenditures, as the name itself suggests. Here too, consideration must be had for the person, the work, and the purpose. For it does not befit just any person to make great expenditures; nor is the one who makes them properly **magnificent** unless they do so for great and splendid works, and for noble ends.

<margin>Commentary on Ethics, Book 4, chapter 5.</margin>
Therefore, most of these actions are performed **for the Public Good, and for the Divine Power** <note>original Greek: *εἰς τὸ κοινὸν, καὶ εἰς τὸ θεῖον* (eis to koinon, kai eis to theion)</note>, as **Aristotle** advises.

15. ***Magnanimity*** <note>From the Latin *magnanimitas*, literally "greatness of soul."</note> is the first of those virtues which are referred back to ***Fortitude***, or, if you prefer, to ***Endurance***. Indeed, ***Magnanimity*** is sufficiently understood from the character of the ***Magnanimous man***, who is described somewhat more fully by ***Aristotle***. The essence of this character consists mostly in this: <margin>Aristotle, *Nicomachean Ethics*, Book 4, Chapters 7 and 8.</margin> *That he always seeks to do great things and for the sake of great things, and those things from which great honor is acquired.* Hence it is that he is a *seeker of great danger* <note>original: "μεγαλοκίνδυνος" (megalokindynos)</note> rather than a *seeker of frequent danger* <note>original: "πυκνοκίνδυνος" (pyknokindynos)</note>; he involves himself in great dangers rather than common ones. Nor is he quick to act, but is *something of a slow and delaying person* <note>original: "ἀργός τις καὶ μελλητής" (argos tis kai mellētēs)</note>—a lazy and procrastinating man, so to speak. For great things are not to be undertaken rashly, but only with great deliberation and counsel. Nor is he held by a great zeal for human affairs, since nothing in these is truly great or to be esteemed as such. Above all else, however, he values ***Honor*** as the greatest of human, *external* goods, inasmuch as we attribute honor even to the Divine Power. For the ***Magnanimous man*** is assumed to be endowed with perfect ***Virtue***, whence he considers himself, if anyone else, worthy of honor because of ***Virtue***, which is the most divine gift of all.

But he does not value even ***Honor*** or the opinion of the common people too highly, being content with his own ***Virtue*** alone. Whence he also emerges as an eminent ***Truth-teller*** <note>original: "Parrhesiastes" (from the Greek παρρησιαστής), one who speaks everything freely and boldly.</note>, having a *greater regard for ***Truth*** and duty than for fame*; but he is also *open in his friendship and open in his hatred* <note>original: "φανερόφιλος καὶ φανερόμισος" (phanerophilos kai phaneromisos)</note>, carrying friendship and enmity in an open breast, as ***Ennius*** <note>Quintus Ennius, an early Roman poet often cited by later philosophers for his moral maxims.</note> says. For why should such a man seek hiding places?

18. **Constancy** <note>original: *Constantia*</note> is the Virtue by which we are consistent with ourselves everywhere, in both words and deeds.

**Diligence** <note>original: *Diligentia*</note> is the Virtue by which we pursue without delay and with care those things we have undertaken through **Right Reason** <note>The intellectual capacity to determine the moral and correct course of action.</note>.

**Goodness of Spirit** <note>original: *Εὐψυχία* (*Eupsychia*)</note>, or **Vivacity**, is defined by *Andronicus* as *a certain firm and lively aptitude of the soul for completing its works*.

For this reason, it seems to differ very little from **Diligence**. **Manliness of Spirit** <note>original: *Ἀῤῥενότης* (*Arrhenotes*)</note>, or **Vigor**, is for him a *disposition that renders us sufficient in the labors of Virtue*.

**Nobility** <note>original: *Ἀνδραγαθία* (*Andragathia*)</note>, or **Virility**, is finally defined by him as *the virtue of a man by which he conducts himself zealously regarding public works*. Indeed, he establishes that its chief duties are to make us fearless concerning death, bold regarding dangers, and to prefer dying through **Virtue** than living through disgrace. These are clearly parts of **Fortitude** <note>original: *Fortitudo*; the virtue of courage and strength of mind.</note>.

Which is, according to the Emperor Marcus <margin>*To Himself* <note>The personal journals of Marcus Aurelius, now commonly known as the *Meditations*.</note> book 12, section 27.</margin>, *to show oneself, on any given occasion, as just, prudent, and simply following God.*

### Ethical Handbook. Book II.

...lacks. Indeed, that some introduce Virtue as being flanked on both sides by opposing Vices, and placed like a **Rose between two nettles** (as is commonly said by our people), certainly presents the appearance of a very beautiful spectacle, but it is a view that cannot hold true for all Virtues.

2. For to that part of **Justice** by which one takes only what is rightfully owed to them, **greed** <note>original: πλεονεξία (pleonexia); the vice of always wanting more than one's fair share.</note> is clearly opposed on one side, which is the vice of seizing more for oneself than is just. But if someone takes less for themselves than what is rightfully owed to them (which might be called **taking less** <note>original: μειονεξία (meionexia); the act of accepting less than one's due.</note>), this certainly does not seem to be a vice, but rather a species of either **Generosity** or **Modesty**. Similarly, in paying a reward, if someone returns less than what is owed by agreement, it is a species of **Injustice**, which can be called **underpaying** <note>original: μειονοδοσία (meionodosia).</note>; just as returning the exact amount is an act of **Justice**. However, returning more (which you could call **overpaying** <note>original: πλεονοδοσίαν (pleonodosia).</note>) is not another species of **Injustice**, but rather of **Liberality**. Thus, in buying and selling goods, that "over-weight" and the **make-weight** <note>original: *Mantissa*; an additional amount thrown into a scale for good measure, similar to a "baker's dozen."</note> which some are accustomed to add to find favor with buyers—even though they exceed the weight and measure established by law—nonetheless, this kind of **over-giving** <note>original: πλεονοδοσία (pleonodosia).</note> has nothing of **Injustice** in it.

For according to its own essence it cannot be a "mean," since that moderation (as I just pointed out) exists in the objects with which virtue deals, namely in **actions and passions**. But since, by its very nature, virtue is the best of all things belonging to the human race, and the most excellent power and perfection of our soul, it cannot be defined more correctly than if one calls it **the summit of human nature** <note>original Greek: *τῆς ἀνθρωπίνης φύσεως ἀκρότητα* (tēs anthrōpinēs physeōs akrotēta)</note>, **the peak of human nature, and the supreme Good**. He [Aristotle] speaks more safely and correctly, therefore, where he says that it is the property of Virtue **to find and choose the Mean** <note>original Greek: *τὸ μέσον αἱρέσκειν καὶ αἱρεῖσθαι* (to meson haireskein kai haireisthai)</note>, than where he suggests that Virtue itself is a **Mean** or a **Mediocrity**. 7. Finally, when they say that Virtue is a mean, they understand it to be a mean between two things of the same kind. For thus **Aristotle** illustrates the matter by Arithmetic proportion, both in magnitudes and in numbers; although in these cases he seems to have found **the mean of the thing itself** <note>original Greek: *τὸ μέσον τοῦ πράγματος* (to meson tou pragmatos)</note> rather than **the mean relative to us** <note>original Greek: *τὸ πρὸς ἡμᾶς* (to pros hēmas)</note>. But that they somewhat strive for this **homogeneity** <note>The quality of being of the same kind or nature.</note> is evident from this: that while they want Virtue to be a certain mean, they imply that it participates in the extremes. This is clearly done by **Andronicus** <note>Likely Andronicus of Rhodes, a philosopher who organized Aristotle's works.</note> in Book 3, Chapter 7, where he says that Virtue **is a Middle state between two Vices, falling short of one, but exceeding the other**. Virtue, therefore, is not the mean itself, but the discoverer and chooser of the mean. Nor is the mean itself perceived only in intensity or extension, but is also determined by other circumstances.

<margin>Nicomachean Ethics, book 2, chapter 6.</margin>

For *when it is proper, and concerning what things, and toward whom, and for what purpose, and in what manner it is proper*, that is the mean and the best which belongs to Virtue, as Aristotle says. Hence it seems superfluous and clearly obsessive to chase after this metaphor <note>The metaphor of the "Mean" or middle-ground.</note> in every single instance.

8. It is enough if that which Virtue seeks and chooses is the **Right**. <margin>Great Ethics, book 1, chapter 25, and Nicomachean Ethics, book 2, chapter 5.</margin>

Hence that saying of the **Pythagoreans**: *The Good is uniform, but Evil is multiform*. And correctly does **Andronicus** indicate that this **Right**—which he also calls a **right action** <note>original Greek: κατόρθωμα (katorthōma)</note>—is **something simple and uniform** <note>original Greek: ἁπλοῦν τι καὶ μονοειδὲς (haploun ti kai monoeides)</note>.

For **those things which are congruous are equal**, as Geometers well know.

Therefore, no one should wonder why that **Right Reason** is said to be **according to Prudence** <note>original Latin: *secundum Prudentiam*</note>, since only the prudent person—and no one else—can be imbued with it as far as life and morals are concerned.

And perhaps the virtuous man stands out most of all by seeing the truth in each case, as if he himself were their norm and measure. For nothing extinguishes this Love more than the sense of pleasure and lust.

## Ethical Handbook. Book II.

...[per]fect **Happiness**, or at least a part of it so great that it can keep us safe from all immense torture and free the spirit from all disordered movement and stupor. For whatever either extinguishes the operation of the mind, or necessarily calls it away to worse things and detains it there for a longer time, must likewise take away or greatly diminish our **Happiness**.

12. Among the goods of the *Individual* <note>original Latin: *Suppositi*; in 17th-century scholastic language, this refers to the person as a distinct, underlying subject or being.</note>, it may rightly seem doubtful whether *Liberty* or *Riches* is more excellent. I, however, have always judged that *Riches* should be placed after *Liberty*, especially since Riches imply a certain abundance which a man of integrity can do without without any trouble. Hence, it must be that for him the loss of *Liberty* is a greater blow than the loss of *Riches*, provided that the necessities for living are supplied; and that he would bear it more mildly if those things superfluous to a happy life must be cast off or lost, than if he had to live at the whim of another—whom he could not always obey without some detriment to *Virtue*, since the height of human felicity consists almost entirely in this.

Therefore, neither *Poverty* <note>original Latin: *Inopia*; meaning a lack of resources or wealth.</note> nor even *Servitude* itself are to be greatly feared, provided they are restricted within such limits that they do not hinder the mind in the operations of *Virtue*, nor intercept or extinguish the perception of that pleasure which those more divine senses and thoughts of the soul bring to it—by which it submits itself entirely to God, while in the meantime being suffused with a silent and internal joy from the consciousness of such an amiable...

### Chap. 10. Ethical Handbook.

13. That Nobility is not necessary for **Happiness** is clear from the very nature of Nobility itself, since it is only a shadow of the **Virtue** of ancestors projected onto their descendants. If that shadow is anything at all, how much greater—indeed, how immense—is **Virtue** itself, whose mere shadow scatters glory through so many lasting ages, gilding so many successions and lineages of men with its rays? Where, then, **Virtue** itself is present—of which even the slightest remains are so powerful—what *self-sufficiency* <note>original Greek: *αὐτάρκειαν* (autarkeian); a central Stoic and Aristotelian concept meaning the state of needing nothing else to be happy.</note>, what solid happiness will she herself provide to her possessor? She stands no more in need of nobility than the Sun needs the moonlight, which the Moon borrows from him.

Therefore, bare Nobility—which the Greeks call *good birth* <note>original Greek: *εὐγένειαν* (eugeneian); referring here to mere inherited rank or "well-born" status.</note>—contributes little to **Happiness**. But if the **Virtue** of ancestors is actually passed down to descendants—which is *nobility of spirit* <note>original Greek: *γενναιότης* (gennaiotēs); meaning true excellence of character that is inherited, rather than just a title.</note>—it has an equal, or rather greater, power toward human happiness than **Virtue** lacking nobility.

14. And if Nobility is not necessary for a happy life, much less are *Imperial Power* and *Sovereignties*. For no one would say that only Princes and Magistrates are happy, since they are so few in number compared to the rest of mortals, and since they are gnawed by so many cares and are continually surrounded by such infinite dangers.

## Ethical Handbook. Book II.

...and indeed, human **Friendships** and favor bring a great deal of sweetness and security to human life. **Virtue** cannot be deprived of these, especially if she is accompanied by a perfect *Sincerity* <note>original Latin: *Simplicitas*; in this context, it refers to a lack of guile or "doubleness" in character</note>, and a certain sweetness and kindness of character. Furthermore, all good men are friends to one another; and by the mark of **Virtue**, as if by a certain *token of recognition* <note>original Greek: *ἀναγνωρίσματι* (anagnōrismati); a term used in Greek drama for a physical sign or object that allows long-separated kin to recognize one another</note>, they immediately recognize their affinity and bond. Consequently, bound together as if by a right of blood-kinship, they readily assist one another.

But if it should happen that one must deal only with the wicked, the **Laws** themselves are the protectors of **Virtue**. For political rights aim at the same goal as **Moral Philosophy** itself, as *Aristotle* <margin>Book 1, chapter 2</margin> rightly advises. And "the same good is sought both by the individual man and by the State," as his interpreter *Andronicus Rhodius* <note>A 1st-century BCE philosopher known for organizing Aristotle's works into the system we use today</note> skillfully adds. Therefore, very little will be lacking to a good man for even the most solid happiness, provided that those things which are owed to him—at least by natural law—are duly fulfilled. Even that most famous example of *Damon* and *Pythias* <note>A legendary Greek pair: when Pythias was sentenced to death, Damon took his place in prison so Pythias could settle his affairs, trusting him to return; their loyalty so impressed the tyrant Dionysius that he pardoned them</note> seems to refer not so much to **Friendship** as to **Justice** and **Equity**.

**Virtue**, therefore—especially among good men or in a well-ordered **Commonwealth**—does not seem to require any more favor from men than she can win for herself by her own power.

6. However, to be perfectly honest, injustice is sometimes woven into the **Laws** themselves, especially those which concern religions;

# Chapter 1. Ethical Manual.

**Judgment** <note>original: *Arbitrium*</note> is a more precise term than **Voluntary** or **Spontaneous**, as it encompasses within itself this specific distinction: namely, the power of both acting and not acting. The **Spontaneous**, <margin>Andronicus of Rhodes, Book 3, Chapter 2.</margin> however, is defined simply as: *That whose principle of motion is within the agent who understands the specific circumstances of the action*. For this reason, both that which we do through an ignorance for which we are not responsible, and that which we do under the compulsion of force, is rightly called *akousion* <note>original Greek: *ἀκούσιον*</note> or **Involuntary**.

10. That which is **Spontaneous** in such a way that it is free—allowing us to will or act otherwise—is properly what constitutes **Free Will** <note>original: *Liberi arbitrii*</note>. This state presupposes a free <term>pre-election<note>original: *praeelectionem*. This refers to the act of choosing one path over another after internal deliberation.</note></term> within us; which *Andronicus*, following the thought of *Aristotle*, defines as *A deliberative desire for those things which are in our power*. <margin>Book 3, Chapter 4.</margin> *For those things* (he says) *are the subjects of deliberation, of which a person is the master of both doing and not doing*. And these are the very things he calls *ta eph' hēmin* <note>original Greek: *τὰ ἐφ' ἡμῖν*</note>, or *those things which are in our power*.

When this power concerns things that are base or shameful, it is a kind of **Perfection**; but when it concerns things that are beautiful and honorable, it is a most wretched **Imperfection**. <note>The author suggests that the "power" to choose evil over good is actually a sign of a flawed or unrefined soul, whereas a perfected soul is so aligned with the Good that it "cannot" choose otherwise.</note> Indeed, it is only one step away from Wickedness itself to be able to turn the Will toward any shameful action. Nevertheless, the fact that we *could* have abstained from shameful things—even in those moments when we did not actually abstain—is a perfecting power, and it is of great importance to recognize this capacity within ourselves. We shall therefore easily reveal that this power is innate to the human race through the following brief indicators.

<summary>This page defines Free Will as a "deliberative desire" and distinguishes it from simple spontaneity by the presence of choice (the power to act or not act). The author argues that while the ability to deviate from virtue is a sign of imperfection, the inherent capacity to have chosen better is a vital part of human nature.</summary>

# Chapter 1. Ethical Manual.

...**Choice** <note>original Latin: *Arbitrium*</note> more so than the **Voluntary** or the **Spontaneous**, since it also includes within itself this distinction: namely, the power of acting and of not acting. The **Spontaneous**, however, is simply defined—<margin>Andronicus of Rhodes, Book 3, Chapter 2.</margin>—as *that whose principle is within the agent who knows the individual circumstances in which the action takes place*. Hence, both that which we do through ignorance (of which we ourselves are not the cause) and that which we do when compelled by force are rightly called <term>Involuntary<note>original Greek: *ἀκούσιον* (*akousion*)</note></term> or **Unwilling**.

10. But the **Spontaneous** which is so free that we are able to will and act otherwise—that is properly called **Free Choice**, which assumes a free "pre-election" <note>A prior choice or preference made before action.</note> within us; which *Andronicus*, following the mind of *Aristotle*, defines as a *Deliberative desire for those things that are within our power.* <margin>Book 3, Chapter 4.</margin> *For those things* (he says) *are what fall under deliberation, of which a person is the master of both doing and not doing.* And these are the very things he calls <term>matters in our power<note>original Greek: *τὰ ἐφ' ἡμῖν* (*ta eph' hēmin*). A central concept in ancient ethics referring to things we can control, like our opinions and choices, versus external events.</note></term>.

When this power concerns things that are shameful, it is a kind of **Perfection** <note>Meaning the perfection of our self-control in resisting evil.</note>; but when it concerns things that are beautiful and noble, it is a most wretched **Imperfection**. For it is only one step away from wickedness itself to be able to turn the Will toward any shameful action whatsoever. Nevertheless, to have been able to abstain from shameful things—even in those moments when we did *not* actually abstain—is a perfecting power, and it is of great importance to recognize it within ourselves. We shall easily reveal that this power is innate to the human race by these very brief proofs.

<summary>This page defines "Free Choice" as a deliberate desire for things within our control, distinguishing it from mere spontaneous action. It argues that while the ability to choose evil is a moral imperfection, the inherent power to have chosen otherwise is a vital part of human nature.</summary>

### Ethical Manual. Book III.

11. For there is no need to bring forward other arguments here than those we noted above in the chapters on the *Interpretation of the Passions*. For the fact that our **Conscience** <note>original Latin: *Conscientia*</note> frequently bites <note>A common philosophical metaphor for the "sting" or "remorse" of conscience.</note> us after we have committed something that we had decided upon before due deliberation, and with a certain wavering of the mind, makes it clearly evident from this alone that we sometimes act in such a way that we could have both willed and acted otherwise. This is precisely what we call **Free Choice** <note>original Latin: *Liberum arbitrium*</note>.

12. The reasoning regarding **Repentance** <note>original Latin: *Poenitentia*; can also be translated as "penitence."</note> is entirely similar. For when we are carried away by some emotion and, while fully aware and knowing, commit acts against the reason of **Honor** <note>original Latin: *Honesti*; in this context, it refers to the "Honestum," the standard of moral goodness and virtue.</note>, we are said to later repent of them. We do not grieve over them as if they were **Misfortunes** <note>original Latin: *Infortunia*</note>; yet such misdeeds would be of that nature if it had never been within our power to escape them, but we had always been destined for them by some divine **Fate** <note>original Latin: *Fato*</note> or a necessary chain of causes, or irresistibly determined toward them. Indeed, no one repents of **Misfortunes**, but of **Sins** <note>original Latin: *Peccatorum*</note>, because they were committed by one's own fault when one could have acted otherwise. To repent of sins which were never in our power to avoid is just as if someone were to weep profusely over their own wickedness and malice, and perform a solemn penance because they were not created an Angel or born a Prince; as we also suggested above.

### Chapter 2. Ethical Manual.

...or we forgive, and finally pity others—if the human race were deprived of **Free Choice** <note>original Latin: *Libero arbitrio*</note>, and it were not situated within our power to flee those things which are shameful, and to embrace those which are honorable and beautiful? ### Ethical Manual. Book III.

...or as long as something appears good or even best to someone in their given circumstances, it necessarily determines their will to embrace it. This is because there is no underlying reason or cause to call them away from it or to suspend their action. Since the **Human Will** <note>original Latin: *Voluntas humana*</note> is constructed in such a way that it can be turned this way or that by the "weight" of various matters, it seems impossible for it not to incline toward whatever momentum impels it, especially when there is nothing in the opposing scale to balance it. Even if there is something else in the balance, the **greater apparent good** <note>original: *majus bonum apparens*; a central concept in ethics suggesting that the mind is naturally drawn to what it perceives as the most beneficial option at the time.</note> will always outweigh the rest. No reason can be given why someone would be moved more by a lesser good than by no good at all. For if the lesser outweighs the greater in the scales of reason, then there is nothing truly causing that "outweighing," and thus our reason and **Choice** <term>Choice: translated from *electio*; the rational act of selecting one possibility over another.</term> would be moved by nothing—which is the height of absurdity.

Therefore, the will always inclines toward the greater apparent good, and is consequently necessarily determined toward one single path. From this, it clearly follows that there is no **Free Choice** <note>original: *Liberum arbitrium*</note> within us, and that we could never have acted differently than we actually did.

## Chapter 2. Ethical Manual.

...because it is necessary. From this, those things which are contingent <note>Events that may or may not happen, depending on circumstances or choice.</note> and which proceed from a free Principle are also proven to be so by divine testimony. For we ought not to confine Divine **Omniscience** <note>original: *Omniscientiam*; God's attribute of knowing all things.</note> within narrower limits than those in which His **Omnipotence** <note>original: *Omnipotentia*; God's attribute of being all-powerful.</note> is enclosed; for everyone confesses with one voice that He is capable of whatever does not involve a contradiction.

To resolve this difficulty briefly, then: the Foreknowledge of contingent effects, or those proceeding from a free principle, either implies a contradiction or it does not. If it implies a contradiction, such effects are not Objects of Divine Omniscience, and therefore are not determined by it, nor can they be rightly judged to be so determined. If it does not imply a contradiction, we acknowledge by that very fact that Divine Foreknowledge and **Free Will** <note>original: *Liberum arbitrium*</note> are by no means <term>incompatible</term> <note>original Greek: *ἀσύστατα* (asustata); literally "things that cannot stand together."</note>, but that both can conveniently coexist. Therefore, in either case, it follows that no solid argument can be deduced from Divine Foreknowledge against the Freedom of the human Will.

3. The sense of the other difficulty is almost entirely resolved in that proverbial little verse,

### CHAP. III.

### *Theorems serving the acquisition of Virtues in general.*

1. The Theorems or Precepts which serve the acquisition of Virtue are either **General** or **Special**. The **General** ones are reduced to these three heads: First, it must be demonstrated that we ought to apply ourselves to acquiring Virtue; second, that it is in our power to acquire Virtue; and thirdly, finally, we shall add certain warnings or precepts—few indeed, but those which we consider most effective for acquiring Virtue.

2. **That we ought to apply ourselves to Virtue, and flee Vices**, is clearly known to us from the sense of our own **Conscience**. But it is also manifest from the law of **Reason**, which God has implanted in us, that we are obligated to the duties of Virtue. For that **Intellect** or **Right Reason** <note>original: *recta Ratio*; the author views human reason as a divine spark that provides a reliable guide for moral behavior.</note> within us is something superior, which all other faculties are bound by natural right to obey. # CHAP. 3. *Enchiridion Ethicum.*

...and of **Right Reason** is entirely the same. For Virtue, in every single action, seeks nothing except what is simply the best—that is, what is in harmony with Right Reason, as we have taught above. Since, however, this Law (whether of Virtue or of Right Reason) is not something **positive** <note>In this context, "positive" refers to laws created by human decree or specific historical circumstances, rather than those inherent in nature.</note> or arbitrary, but belongs to an eternal and immutable nature, it is necessary that we be bound to obey its ordinances and precepts by an eternal and unbreakable bond.

3. Furthermore, by the common Law of Nature, all things are bound to do what is "their own"—that is, those things which are in harmony with their own specific nature. Humans, therefore, ought to lead a human life, not a beast-like one; yet a man's life would be entirely beastly if it lacked the fruit of Virtue and Right Reason.

Whatever within us is lower than Virtue and Right Reason is not our "true self," but a certain beast joined to us—the <term>lion-like and the bestial</term> <note>original Greek: *to leontōdes kai thēriōdes*</note>, as **Plotinus** <note>A major Neoplatonic philosopher whose works deeply influenced the author.</note> calls it—which we must subdue and make obedient to the true human. # Handbook of Ethics. Book III.

It clearly seems to be placed within our power to move or stop this external **puppet** <term>puppet: the original Greek term used here is *Neurospaston*, referring to a string-controlled marionette. Indeed, various desires and aversions easily creep up on us; but it is within our own power either to withdraw ourselves from objects that please us too much, or to move ourselves toward those things in which we take less delight.

If we do this constantly in matters of indifference—so far as bodily health and social politeness allow—we shall increase the powers of our **Free Will** in a wonderful manner, as I have said, and at last reclaim ourselves for perfect freedom. For unless we indulge our Desires and Aversions, they will eventually grow weak and easily obey **Reason**.

But it can also be proved by another reason that it is within our power to eventually turn out as upright men, endowed with true **Virtue**. For it is clearly placed in our power to be sincere: since by *Sincerity* I mean nothing else here but a constant resolution to do all those things which are in our power toward acquiring true Virtue. ### Manual of Ethics. Book III.

...*to meditate upon the death of the perishable Body, and upon the Immortality of our Soul.* For it has very great power to extinguish all those desires that end in this mortal body, to seriously consider that, in a short time, this corporeal and visible personality must be scattered into wandering atoms, and all those things which belong to this physical structure must be left behind forever—such as Riches, Honors, and the pleasures of the Body. And therefore, it is more advisable to wean ourselves early from all perishable things, and little by little to <term>unsew and tear ourselves away <gloss>original: dissuere & divellere, a metaphor for separating the soul's attachment from the physical body.</gloss></term> from the agreement and society of this earthly flesh; and instead to accustom our Soul to purer and more divine pleasures and operations which do not depend upon the body. <margin>Pliny, Natural History, Book 7, Chapter 50.</margin>
13. Nor is it a disease to die in this way through wisdom—as *Pliny* <note>Pliny the Elder, a Roman author who famously expressed a more skeptical or materialistic view of death in his encyclopedic work.</note> wrongly hints at somewhere—but rather it is the most perfect Wisdom. For he is truly wise who looks forward into the distance, and does not allow present pleasures to be occupied and overwhelmed by an infinite series of evils. For this reason, we must apply every nerve to Virtue, which alone—like the Soul itself—is immortal, and is the Soul's proper ornament and perfection. Indeed, there is such a great kinship between Virtue and the immortality of the Soul, that a certain sense and perception of Immortality is, for the most part, bred into our Soul along with Virtue itself.

### Manual of Ethics. Book III.

*Not to be swept away.* <note>original Greek: *Μὴ ἀπορπηθῆναι*; a warning against being carried away by sudden impulses or passions.</note> The first is a warning from **Marcus Antoninus** <note>Also known as Marcus Aurelius, the Roman Emperor and Stoic philosopher.</note>, the second from **Epictetus**. Both indeed teach that *we ought not to leap forth or be hurried toward any task rashly and without deliberation.*

20. The second rule is, *Never to commit anything against one's own Conscience*, but to preserve it whole and untainted in the smallest matters as well as the greatest, and constantly to observe that most excellent precept of <margin>Enchiridion, chapter 75.</margin> **Epictetus**: *Whatever seems best, let that be an inviolable Law for you.* For once a person has learned to prefer a lesser good over a greater one (even while their Conscience remains technically intact), it is to be feared that they will eventually learn to cast away that remaining lesser good in the same way, and pollute themselves entirely with filth and vice. For the portion of good they first threw away was just as much a "good" as the remainder they are soon to discard. Therefore, we must work diligently to shrink back from every kind of baseness. For a present sin paves the way for a future one, and our individual <term>Admissions</term> <note>Latin: *Admissa*; here meaning faults, sins, or things allowed to pass.</note> are like so many rings of that iron or adamantine Chain, by which we will eventually be bound in the inextricable knots of Wickedness and eternal darkness.

21. The third rule is, *That in every object or situation we encounter, we should seek the exercise of Virtue.* For whatever happens can be done either rightly or wrongly, gracefully or ungracefully, justly or unjustly, with reason and moderation, or beyond all reason and measure. ### Chapter 5. Ethical Handbook.

5. However, for anyone to be so "just" that they only keep themselves within the limits of human laws is a matter of **Cunning** rather than true **Justice**. Some prefer to call this *Fraud* and *Cunning* by the name of *Prudence*, stretching a beautiful title over the worst of Vices; the assembly of true Virtues shrinks back from this no less than honest and modest Matrons shrink from the company of a most foul prostitute. Others applaud themselves for this vice as if it were a select specimen of wit and sharpness: as if indeed anyone were born so stupid that they could not deceive through lies and hypocrisy if they wished. He who cannot deceive when he wishes must indeed be of the slowest wit of all; but he who wishes to do so when he can is of the most vile and abject wit. However, he who does not wish to deceive even though he is able, he alone possesses a great and lofty mind, and he alone breathes true *Prudence* and *Generosity* <note>original: Generositatem; here referring to the nobility of character or "high-born" spirit rather than just financial giving.</note>.

*Humanity* <term>Humanitas: In this context, it refers to the virtue of benevolence, kindness, and the recognition of our shared human nature.</term> indeed must be cultivated above all other Virtues. For we are all held together, in a certain way, by a common bond of kinship and equality; nor should one man be thought to far surpass another, since we all share equally in **Death** and **Immortality**, in **Passions** and **Reason**. Therefore, he who looks down upon, despises, neglects, or treats another less humanely, seems to have lost the rights and privileges of human Nature, and to have openly passed judgment against himself—implying that it would matter little, surely, if he himself were treated in the same way under the same circumstances. Since he is a man, if he wished some immunity to be reserved for himself here above others, this would truly be a stupid and ridiculous pride and arrogance of mind.

No one, therefore, however humble their fortune may be, ought to be despised or treated insultingly, provided they are an upright person and have not lost the rights of human Nature through their own fault. <margin>*"Enter, for the gods are here also," said Heraclitus.* <note>The philosopher Heraclitus supposedly said this to visitors who found him warming himself by a kitchen stove, suggesting that the divine is found in humble places.</note></margin> This should be considered most true of the heart of even the poorest person, provided they are upright: whom we ought, accordingly, based on the shared privileges of human nature, always to receive with due love and respect, as if they were a kind of sacred and divine Living Being.

### CHAP. VII.
### *On the acquisition of the Virtues which are related to Fortitude.*

1. The virtues that are grouped under **Fortitude** <note>The author uses "Fortitude" here not just as physical bravery, but as a moral strength and firmness of soul.</note> are **Magnanimity**, **Generosity**, **Gentleness**, **Constancy**, and **Diligence**; likewise, **Vivacity**, **Presence of Mind**, **Strenuousness**, and **Manliness** <note>original: "Virilitas"; in this context, it refers to a mature, vigorous strength of character.</note>.

**Magnanimity** <note>Literally "greatness of soul."</note> is commended because it does not distract the mind with many petty matters, but causes it to aspire to the best and greatest things, which are few. It knows how to rightly estimate the excellence of human nature, and does not wish to abuse that nature by pursuing the smallest and most vile things. Since, therefore, nothing is greater or more excellent than God and **Virtue**, it strengthens and establishes our mind and will in cultivating these, and does not allow them to scatter or wander toward common objects.

This virtue also shares something in common with **Magnificence** <note>A term from classical ethics referring to the habit of doing great and noble deeds on a large or public scale.</note>: that its noble deeds are especially beneficial to the Public, and they adorn the ages and the History of the world.

2. Moreover, what most commends ***Frugality*** is that it is either the mother or the companion of **Sobriety**, and the banisher of Disease and Poverty. Thus we see that true ***Frugality*** can actually be underpinned by a certain ***Generosity*** and an honorable ***Greatness of soul*** <term>Magnitudo animi: the quality of being high-minded and noble; often translated as Magnanimity</term>.

9. Regarding those goods which relate to the Body—such as **Strength**, **Agility**, **Health**, and **Beauty**—it is true that **Strength** seems to be a gift of Nature rather than of Virtue; nevertheless, its preservation must also be credited to Virtue. Indeed, it does not seem at all unlikely that the Body, which might otherwise have been weaker, can become much more robust through the exercises of *Endurance*.

**Agility** of the body, however, can be seen not only as a foster-child of Virtue, but even as its true daughter. For *Temperance* <note>meaning moderation in food and drink</note> and *Diligence* usually diminish superfluous body mass and produce a sufficiently large supply of spirits <term>spirits: in 17th-century physiology, these were "animal spirits," subtle fluids thought to flow through the nerves to animate the body</term>. From this, the body’s **Agility** is necessarily born.

11. Therefore, diseases of the body are, for the most part, the effects of the vices of the soul. For unfortunate descendants often pay for the sins of their ancestors, and the diseases of parents—along with their lands and titles—are passed down to their children as if by a certain hereditary right. There is no more effective way for them to cast off and shake off this burden than if they strictly choose to cultivate **Piety** and **Virtue**.

Therefore, it is in vain that you threaten an upright man with the filth of a prison, and in vain with solitude: for he cannot but dwell in splendor whom the Divine presence always illuminates and surrounds with light; nor can he be alone, with whom all the Virtues and a good Conscience converse so freely.

### Ch. 9. Manual of Ethics.

Virtue alone brings about and preserves true **Friendships**; when it has put itself forward (as **Laelius** discusses excellently on that matter in **Cicero's** work), and has shown its own light, and has seen and recognized the same light in another, it moves toward it, and in turn receives that which is in the other, from which **Love** or **Friendship** blazes forth. And he adds further: *To love is nothing other than to cherish the very person whom you love, with no need, no utility sought.* <note>original: "Amare nihil aliud esse nisi eum ipsum diligere quem ames, nulla indigentia, nulla utilitate quæsita." More is warning against "fair-weather" friends who only value others for what they can get out of them.</note>

From this it follows that no protection of human life can be greater than Virtue itself, since it alone by itself has such great power of enticing men to love and to winning their **Benevolence**, which all honorable and timely duties must necessarily accompany.

4. Indeed, since we see that this hope of Immortality shone forth and was known even to the Pagans of old, it must by no means be excluded from Moral Philosophy. It serves as the most certain and just compensator for all those external evils by which innocent Virtue—whether through some mysterious fate, or through the envy and wickedness of villainous men—might be vexed and afflicted in this life. Relying on this hope alone, therefore, the upright and magnanimous man holds everything that can befall a human being beneath him; looking down upon these things, he despises human accidents. Being free from all blame, he considers nothing to belong to him except Virtue and immortality. In this way, **Cicero** somewhere brilliantly boasts concerning the strength of Virtue.

### Chap. 10. Manual of Ethics.
#### Page 235

...nevertheless, he <note>Referring to Socrates, who famously claimed to know nothing ("I know that I know nothing"), yet held firm to the immortality of the soul.</note> wished to seem wise in this alone: that while he was uncertain in other matters, he doubted nothing regarding the immortality of the Soul. 6. Therefore, if in any matter concerning *External Goods* <note>In classical ethics, "External Goods" refer to things like wealth, health, and reputation, as opposed to the "Internal Goods" of the soul, such as virtue.</note> it might seem that Virtue stands in our way, it must nevertheless be borne with a calm and constant mind, since such a massive compensation awaits us after the brief course of this life. Nay, indeed, we ought rather to count as gain whatever we suffer in external goods—those of the Body, for instance, and of Fortune; inasmuch as, if we wish to use such losses rightly and wisely, and as the matter itself prompts us, however much is taken away from those external Goods, just as much and more is added to the internal goods of the Soul.

Since, moreover, those *external Goods* are mortal and fleeting, just like the Body itself, while *Internal* ones are no less immortal and eternal than the Soul itself, we ought indeed to be much more confirmed by these facts: that the things we suffer in the body or in fortunes should be called gains rather than losses and misfortunes; and that we become more enriched and wealthy from them rather than being in any way mutilated or diminished.

### Ch. 10. Manual of Ethics.

...yet he <note>Referring to Socrates, who famously claimed to know nothing except the fact of his own ignorance.</note> wished to seem wise in this one thing alone: that, while uncertain of other matters, he doubted nothing regarding the immortality of the Soul. For concerning this subject (as *Laelius* testifies in the works of Cicero), he did not say one thing now and another then, as he did with most topics, but always maintained the same: *That the souls of men are divine, and that a return to heaven lies open to them once they have departed from the body; and that this path is the most direct for every person who is most excellent and just.* <note>original: "Animos hominum esse divinos, iisque cum è corpore exiissent reditum ad cælum patere, optimoque & justissimo cuique expeditissimum." This is a famous passage from Cicero’s "De Amicitia" (On Friendship), where Laelius discusses the teachings of Socrates.</note>

6. Therefore, if in any matter concerning **external Goods** <term>external Goods<gloss>In classical philosophy, these are things outside the soul's direct control, such as wealth, reputation, health, or physical safety.</gloss></term> Virtue should seem to stand in our way, it must nevertheless be endured with an even and constant mind, since so great a recompense awaits us after the brief course of this life. Indeed, we ought rather to count as gain whatever we suffer in external goods—namely, those of the Body and of Fortune; for if we wish to use such losses rightly and wisely, and as the situation itself advises us, then however much is taken away from these external Goods, just as much and more is added to the **internal goods** of the Soul.

Since these *external Goods*, like the Body itself, are mortal and perishable, while *Internal goods* are no less immortal and eternal than the Soul itself, we ought to be much more strengthened by this realization: that the losses we suffer in body or in fortune should be called "gains" rather than "damages" or "misfortunes." We should see ourselves as becoming more enriched and wealthy from such experiences, rather than being in any way mutilated or diminished.

### Manual of Ethics. Book III.

...it would be as if someone, having paid a price a hundred times less than the value of the thing he bought, were nevertheless to complain that he was made poorer by this transaction and that his wealth was thereby diminished. So, indeed, it seems to me equally discordant and absurd if anyone should bring complaints against **Divine Providence** <term>Divine Providence<gloss>The belief that God or a higher power guides the universe and human affairs toward a good end.</gloss></term> on account of what he suffers in external goods. For from those losses and injuries, so great an addition can be made to the internal goods of the soul—which truly constitute the greatest part of human happiness—which is measured and defined not by the briefest span of this life, but by the eternal ages of immortality. 

Thus, if anyone wishes to be truly wise, they should not so much shrink from harsh and adverse circumstances as recognize and embrace them as gifts from the most wise God, and as the greatest and most effective instruments for perfecting the Virtues.

For these trials test the powers of the soul, and they scour and wipe away all its vice and rust; <note>The author uses the metaphor of "rust" (rubiginem) to describe the moral decay or stagnation that occurs when the soul is too comfortable; adversity acts as a polish.</note> they engender within us *Prudence*, *Fortitude*, *Sincerity*, and every virtue whatsoever. Since, therefore, those external evils are so useful, they ought to be considered tolerable, just as all health-giving medicines are.

# Chapter 10. Manual of Ethics.

<margin>Manual, chapter 10.</margin>

<margin>Tusculan Disputations, Book 2.</margin>
Regarding this matter, *Cicero* <note>The Roman statesman and orator; More cites his "Tusculan Disputations," a series of books on grief, pain, and the soul.</note> speaks excellently, as he does on all things: *Pain seems to be the sharpest adversary of Virtue; it brandishes burning torches; it threatens to weaken courage, greatness of soul, and patience.* Yet pain could not achieve this so frequently unless we ourselves were at fault. For a nature rightly established and well-imbued is something invincible. But we, as Cicero justly complains, have infected the mind with shadows, luxuries, leisure, sluggishness, and sloth; we have softened it, charmed by opinions and bad habits.

9. Moreover, it is manifest that it is not beyond the powers of human nature to take up even the greatest pains by our own will. This is clear from the fact that, whether through the desire for empty glory, or from the force of some custom or superstition, many have indeed endured very great and intolerable pains.

### Chapter 10. Manual of Ethics.

21. But so that no deception is done to **Religion**, I will say openly and freely what I feel: namely, that almost all those excellent things *concerning God, the Soul, and Virtue* found in the writings of ancient Philosophers, or recorded from the sayings and deeds of the most excellent Pagans, must be credited to either the most ancient doctrine of the Church of God, the ancient **Cabbala** <term>Kabbalah; here referring to a supposed ancient, universal wisdom tradition passed down from the time of Moses</term>, or to the eternal Son of God, the **LOGOS** <term>Logos; the Divine Word or Reason through whom the world was created</term>. It is He who, from all past ages, has imbued every individual with some sense of virtue—and indeed, has granted some a fuller and sharper sense of integrity than others.

*For this is that light which enlightens every man coming into this world* <note>A translation of the Latin quote from the Gospel of John 1:9</note>, as the Christian oracles testify. Moreover, ancient writers—both sacred and secular—eagerly confirm with one voice that **Pythagoras** drew his wisdom from Hebrew sources. Furthermore, it seems too obvious for anyone to doubt that the chief part of this wisdom *concerning God, the immortality of the Soul, and concerning Life and morals* was passed down to **Plato**, then soon to the **Stoa** <note>The Stoic school of philosophy, known for self-control and fortitude</note> and the **Peripatus** <note>The Peripatetic school, founded by Aristotle</note>, and later overflowed into almost the entire world.

Therefore, just as the distinguished **Virtue** and **Wisdom** of many Pagans <note>original: *Ethnicorum*; referring here to the non-Christian philosophers of antiquity, such as Socrates or Plato</note> illustrate in no small measure the power and kindness of Divine Providence—which penetrates all things and flows far and wide—so indeed they cannot obscure the glory of the Church. **Section 9.** For virtue arises out of the passions, and once born, it is in turn constituted along with them. **Section 2.** ...like a certain defensive or even a combative spirit toward those nearby. It is necessary for every virtue to possess these three elements: reason, power, and choice. Reason <note>original: λόγον / *logon*</note> is that by which the virtue judges and contemplates; power <note>original: δύναμιν / *dynamin*</note> is that by which it resists and prevails; and choice <note>original: προαίρεσιν / *proairesin*</note> is that by which it embraces and loves.

And as the man of practical wisdom <note>original: *phronimos*; an individual possessing 'phronesis' or practical discernment</note> would define it.
A true, practical disposition accompanied by reason concerning what is good and bad for a human being.
**Section 11.** For the person of high character <note>original: *spoudaios*; an excellent or serious person</note> judges each thing rightly, and in each thing the truth appears to them. For according to each disposition there are things that are specific, noble, and pleasant. And the person of high character perhaps differs most in seeing the truth in each case, being as it were the rule and measure of them. But for the many, deception seems to occur because of pleasure; for it appears to be a good when it is not.

Letter of More to a Distinguished Man
M 6
<meta>catchword: But</meta>

# LETTER
## Of H. MORE to a DISTINGUISHED MAN

-> WHICH <-
-> *contains a Defense for* DESCARTES, *and which* <-
-> *can serve as an Introduction* <-
-> *to the whole Cartesian Philosophy.* <-

<margin>
I.
That he does not embrace all Cartesian ideas without selection.
</margin>
You ask a great thing of me, Distinguished Sir <note>original: "V. C.", an abbreviation for *Vir Clarissimus*, a formal Latin honorific for a respected scholar or gentleman.</note>: namely, that I deliver my opinion on the <term>Triumvirate</term> <note>A group of three powerful individuals; here, More refers to the three most famous philosophers of his century, likely including Descartes, Gassendi, and Hobbes.</note> of philosophers most distinguished in this century. Regarding two of these, I can determine nothing at all, insofar as I have not yet read them through; nor do I believe it would be worth my while to ever read them through. Indeed, I wonder that you ask me what I think of that third one <note>René Descartes (1596–1650), the French philosopher and mathematician.</note>, since I have publicly testified more than once to the high regard in which I hold him. But while you further inquire for what reasons especially I have so eagerly embraced his philosophy, that somewhat persistent questioning provides me with the subject-matter for a fuller response. But the matter stands quite differently than you suspect. Wherefore it is necessary to summon some higher and more divine cause than Matter and purely Mechanical Motion for this work, if those triangular little columns are to be twisted into a screw-like form so skillfully, with such constant craftsmanship, and intended for such useful ends.

For it would be more in accordance with mechanical laws that they should bore a path for themselves through the air (even if we imagined it to be somewhat thicker), and lose their motion and force by spending them on these efforts, rather than that they should, as if by design, strive for a return and direct their course to the other pole so far distant. For once they have projected themselves from the magnetic parts of the Earth into the air, they are immediately enclosed by parts of the air that are in every way similar to one another, as they are adjacent to each other. From this it is manifest that nothing corporeal <note>That is, nothing made of physical matter or following the laws of impact and motion alone.</note> can be the cause of why these particles—wrapped in this way by homogeneous parts of air on all sides—should break out here rather than there, or why they would prefer to return rather than finish their path in a straight line or be carried upward; but that there underlies some deeper and more **divine Principle** which calls back the wanderers, and which [rules] their motions and courses...

Finally, to this **cumin-splitting** <note>original: *κυμιοπρισίαν* (kuminopristia). A Greek idiom for extreme stinginess or "hair-splitting" precision.</note> or **Mathematical hair-splitting** <note>original: *μικρολογίαν* (mikrologian). Two of this kind occur to me. 

The **first** is that neither **Spirits** <note>original: *Genios*. Here meaning non-material beings or guiding intelligences.</note> nor **human Souls** can move matter, but can only determine its motion toward this or that direction; since it is asserted quite without evidence that any **active and operative Essence** (which is how **spiritual substance** is regarded by everyone) has the power of restraining, stopping, and governing moved matter, and yet could never have even the slightest power to move that same matter in any way. 

The **other** is that a **Body** which imparts motion to another body always loses as much from its own motion as it imparts to the other, and that the very same amount it loses passes into the other body. I believe I could very easily refute this, if I had the time, from a consideration of the so-called **Mechanical Powers** <term>Mechanical Powers: The classical simple machines (lever, pulley, etc.) where force and distance are traded; More suggests these prove that motion isn't a simple "fluid" poured from one cup to another</term>.

...natural, and that upward motion is innate to fire <note>More is mocking an Aristotelian explanation where objects move simply because it is their "nature" to do so.</note>. It is established from her phases <note>The changing visible shapes of the planet, similar to the Moon’s phases, which proved it orbited the Sun.</note> that **Venus** completes her circuits both on this side and the other side of the **Sun**; and the same reasoning applies to **Mercury**. Furthermore, no one has yet doubted that **Mars**, **Jupiter**, and **Saturn** are carried around the Sun. It is therefore manifest that these five **Planets** go and return around the Sun.

Next, we must ask whether they move by cutting a path for themselves through the matter of the **ether** <note>The subtle, fluid substance believed to fill all space.</note>, or whether they are carried around by the motion of the ether itself. It is clear that the first cannot happen; the resistance of the celestial matter would hinder such swift crossings of the Planets, and they would lose their motion in a very short time by transferring it to the fluid ether itself. 

The remaining conclusion, therefore, is that they are carried around by the motion of the ether itself, and that the entire celestial matter in which they float is twisted like a **Vortex** <note>Descartes' theory that planets are carried like straws in a whirlpool of cosmic dust/fluid.</note> around the Sun itself. Finally, let us investigate what happens to the **Earth**, which is undoubtedly found within the limits of this Vortex. Will it stand still in this rapid river, or will it be moved? By what hooks, by what ropes and anchors, shall it be held back in this deep sea? But let us imagine it held by some supernatural force...

...of forming [them] with thin and delicate skill. 
<margin>interposed within them.</margin> 
For the gaps were too wide, and the particles themselves too hard, and perhaps not broad enough to be bored into that twisted, spiral shape; indeed, any matter consisting of a coarser thread or texture than that most subtle matter of all would be far less fit to receive these tiny little holes—which must nevertheless be carved out with the most precise skill—than raw oak or ash would be for carving the likenesses of Emperors in the same cramped space where they are typically engraved on the most precious gems. In this way, he clearly demonstrated to himself once again that the magnetic crusts of the **Earth** <note>original: "Terræ"</note> consist of the matter of the **first element** <term>First element: In Cartesian physics, the finest, fastest-moving matter that makes up the sun and stars.</term>. Since he could not find a sufficient abundance of this matter to build the Earth anywhere outside the centers of the **Vortices** <term>Vortices: The massive whirlpools of cosmic matter that Descartes believed carried planets around stars.</term>, it was necessary that he place the original matter of the Earth in the very axis of some Vortex. In this way, the Planet could be a **Magnet** <note>original: "Magnes"</note> after it had ceased to be a Sun or a **Fixed Star**.

<margin>30. Descartes’ modest and sober [character].</margin>
30. If, therefore, **Descartes** <note>original: "Cartesius"</note> was "insane," it must be said that he was surely insane with the greatest of reason. But he did not actually go so far into insanity—nor did any of his followers, as far as I know—as to conclude anything more from such brilliant evidence than that the nature of things is so arranged *as if* this Earth, of which we are inhabitants, had once been a Sun or a Fixed Star. You see the character of Descartes: how cautious and modest it is, and how solid and sober in every respect.

...by measuring the circuits of the stars <note>original: "stellarum [circuitus]"; the word completes from the previous page</note>, who finally, by weighing everything—both from the attributes of the Supreme Deity and from the proper powers of the **immaterial Orders** <term>Immaterial Orders: A reference to the hierarchy of spiritual beings, such as angels or the human soul, which More believed were as real as physical matter.</term>—has untied all those riddles and knots with which wicked and idle men are accustomed to ensnare devoted worshippers of Religion. ...not so much to cast reproach upon Philosophy as to excuse their own laziness. <note>original: "tam opprobrio Philosophiam afficere, quam suam excusare ignaviam." This completes the marginal note from the previous page.</note>

Scaliger <note>Julius Caesar Scaliger (1484–1558), a celebrated Italian scholar and physician known for his encyclopedic knowledge.</note> retorted to men of this sort, *“Indeed, ignorance usually produces no greater pleasure for the unlearned than a prompt and disdainful contempt.”* <note>original: "Nullam utique majorem ignaris infcitiam parere folere voluptatem, quam expeditum fastidiofumque contemptum."</note> Although certainly that should not be considered so much a pleasure as a certain consolation and soothing of the pain they might feel from the sense of their own loss and the forfeiture of the best things. For a sufficiently great desire for knowing is implanted in all of us by **Nature**, and it includes no small part of natural conscience that we ought not to be stupid and ignorant of things like cattle; yet neither are we bound to the knowledge of impossible or useless things. From this it is manifest that those who complain with such a shrill voice that nothing can be known, do not so much cast reproach on the speculations of **Philosophy** as seek an honorable pretext for themselves, and excuse themselves because they spend almost their whole life in luxury, greed, or ambition.

...intellect, because of what has already been achieved by a man who was certainly clever, but lacked solidity, being someone who had not discovered even the first principles of true **Philosophy**.

<margin>34. Those who think that things serving to cultivate the mind contribute nothing to life, so that they openly profess a brutish existence.</margin>
34. But let us grant, they will say, that **Descartes** <note>René Descartes (1596–1650), the French philosopher whose mechanical physics More initially admired before later becoming more critical.</note> found those true Principles, and brought to light the natural and immediate efficient causes of all **Phenomena**, which that "clever little Greek" <note>original: "Græculus." More likely refers to Aristotle or the Scholastic tradition, which he viewed as overly focused on logic rather than the true nature of things.</note> did not know; what do those things contribute to the conduct of life? If by "the use of life" they mean honors, wealth, and bodily pleasures, I willingly admit he does not contribute much to that. Meanwhile, however, I contend that in the true method of **Philosophizing**, there is found something much more sublime than honors, more precious than wealth, and finally far, far more sweet and pleasant than all the pleasures of the body combined. But as for those who judge that the things which contribute to adorning, feeding, and cheering the human mind with a certain divine joy contribute nothing to human life—truly, they seem to me to have entirely forgotten that they possess a mind, and to openly profess that they lead a life altogether like that of beasts <note>original: "belluinam," referring to a life driven by animal instinct rather than reason.</note>.

Farewell, *Most Distinguished Sir*, and if by chance I have discussed these matters with you more expansively and freely than was proper, forgive this excess of zeal in following your wishes, and continue to love me as you usually do.

->*H. M.* <note>Henry More (1614–1687), the Cambridge Platonist.</note><-
